glossary.gloss: The royal castle and town in Denmark where almost the entire play is set. (A real place: the seaside fortress of Kronborg at Helsingør.)
One of the night sentinels guarding the castle; he and Marcellus have twice seen the dead King's ghost on watch.
A sentinel who is relieved from the night watch at the play's opening.
Hamlet's loyal, level-headed friend and fellow scholar from Wittenberg; the man Hamlet trusts most.
An officer of the watch who, with Barnardo, brings Horatio and then Hamlet to see the Ghost.
No. Often used to correct or push back: "no, on the contrary."
Identify yourself; reveal who you are. A sentry's challenge.
Loyal subjects sworn to serve a lord or king.
The King of Denmark. "Liegemen to the Dane" means loyal subjects of the Danish crown.
Here in its old sense: partners or companions (those sharing the same watch), not competitors.
A shout to get someone's attention; "hey there!"
Imagination; a figment of the mind. Horatio first dismisses the Ghost as mere fantasy.
A ghost; a supernatural appearance of someone, especially the dead.
Confirm what our eyes have seen; prove that we really saw it.
An exclamation of impatient dismissal; "nonsense" or "come off it."
Assault your ears with our story; press the tale on you again.
Yonder; that one over there.
To illuminate; to light up. ("to illume")
Pay attention to it; take note of it.
Distresses or terrifies deeply; literally to tear up as a harrow rips up soil. "It harrows me with fear."
Wrongfully take or occupy. Horatio accuses the Ghost of usurping the night and the dead King's form.
The dead King of Denmark (old Hamlet). Kings were often called by their realm's name.
Here in its old sense: formerly, once, in time past. "Did sometimes march" = used to march.
Command you solemnly; order you under authority.
Walks with a stiff, haughty, menacing stride.
Perceptible to the senses; able to be seen or touched. "Sensible and true avouch" = the firsthand testimony of the senses.
Sworn testimony; a guarantee from one's own witness.
Here, the King of Norway personified — specifically old Fortinbras, whom old Hamlet killed in combat.
A parley; a formal talk or negotiation between enemies. Here, an angry confrontation.
Polish soldiers riding on sledges (sleds) over the ice, whom old Hamlet struck down.
Here in its old sense: exactly, precisely. "Jump at this dead hour" = at exactly this hour.
A warlike, soldierly stride.
The general drift and full range; the overall sense of an opinion.
Foretells or warns of; is an omen of. "Bodes some strange eruption to our state."
A violent disturbance or upheaval coming to the country.
Cannon cast in brass or bronze.
Buying abroad; foreign trade or purchasing, here for weapons of war.
Forced conscription — compelling men (here shipwrights) into service.
Builders of ships.
Here in its old sense: coming, about to happen, in preparation. "What might be toward?"
Both the dead King of Norway (old Fortinbras, slain by old Hamlet) and his hot-headed son, young Fortinbras, now raising an army to win back the lost lands.
The name of both the dead King (a great warrior) and his son, the prince and hero of the play.
Spurred on; goaded into action.
Driven by rivalry and the desire to outdo. "A most emulate pride."
A formal, sealed agreement or contract.
The rules and law governing rank, honor, and combat between nobles.
Legally possessed of; in lawful ownership of (a legal term for holding land).
An equivalent portion or matching share (of land) staked as a wager.
Pledged or staked as a wager.
A binding formal agreement or pact. ("covenant")
Raw, untested spirit or courage — energy not yet disciplined.
The outlying edges or borderlands of Norway.
Greedily gathered together, snapped up indiscriminately (as a shark feeds).
Reckless, lawless men ready for any desperate venture; hired adventurers.
Here in its old sense: appetite for danger, daring, or spirit. "An enterprise that hath a stomach in't."
Compulsory; by force. "Terms compulsatory" = forcible demands.
Great speed and urgency. (Originally the rushed pace of post-riders carrying mail.)
Bustle, commotion, frantic activity.
Here: turn out, fit, or befit. "Well may it sort" = it makes good sense.
Ominous; foreboding disaster.
A tiny speck of dust. "A mote to trouble the mind's eye" = a small thing that disturbs the mind.
Rome at the height of its glory and triumph. ("Palmy" = flourishing, victorious.)
Julius Caesar, the Roman ruler, whose assassination was foreshadowed by strange omens.
Empty, unoccupied. Here the graves stand tenantless because the dead have risen.
Corpses in their burial shrouds.
To make rapid, meaningless, unintelligible sounds.
The Roman god of the sea; "Neptune's empire" is the ocean, ruled by the moon's tides.
The moon, which governs the tides (Neptune's empire).
The Day of Judgment at the end of the world.
A forerunner; an advance sign or warning of events to come.
Forerunners or heralds that announce something coming.
Here in its very common old sense: always, continually, ever. "Preceding still" = always preceding.
Regions or climes; this part of the world. "Our climatures and countrymen."
Here as an interjection: wait, hold on, not so fast. "But soft!"
Look; behold. An exclamation pointing to something.
Step in its path to confront it (also possibly to make the sign of the cross against it).
Strike me down, wither or destroy me (as with a curse).
Secretly aware of; let in on knowledge of. "Privy to thy country's fate."
Here in its old sense: perhaps, by chance, haply. "Which, happily, foreknowing may avoid."
Hoarded up; secretly stored away.
Wealth wrongfully seized or taken by force.
A long-handled spear or pike, a soldier's weapon.
The rooster crowed. By tradition, ghosts must vanish at the cock's crow at dawn.
Wandering out of bounds and straying — said of a spirit roaming where it shouldn't.
Hurries; hastens. "Hies to his confine" = rushes back to where it belongs.
The place a spirit is confined to; its proper bounds.
Proof; a testing that confirms the truth. "Made probation" = proved it true.
In the time approaching that season — here, just before Christmas.
Christmas; the birth of Christ.
The rooster, which sings at daybreak.
No planet exerts a harmful astrological influence. (People believed planets could "strike" with disease or bad luck.)
Fairies bewitch or harm. "No fairy takes" = no fairy can cast a spell.
Holy; made sacred. "So hallow'd and so gracious is the time."
A reddish-brown cloak; here a poetic image of dawn's color spreading over the hills.
That tall hill to the east, where the sun rises.
Silent to us; refusing to speak.
The new King of Denmark: old Hamlet's brother, who murdered him, seized the throne, and married the widowed queen. The play's villain.
Hamlet's mother and Queen of Denmark, who married Claudius (her dead husband's brother) within a month of being widowed.
The King's chief counselor and a long-winded busybody; father of Laertes and Ophelia.
Polonius's son, returning to France; brother of Ophelia.
A Danish courtier sent as ambassador to Norway.
A Danish courtier sent with Voltemand as ambassador to Norway.
The memory is still fresh and recent.

glossary.term: contracted in one brow of woe
glossary.gloss: Drawn together into a single frown of grief — the whole kingdom mourning as one.
Good judgment struggled against natural feeling (grief).
Former sister-in-law. "Sometime" = formerly. Claudius means Gertrude, once his brother's wife.
A widow holding a joint or shared right to the kingdom; here, the queen who brings the realm with her in marriage.
Favorable, joyful, promising good fortune. Paired here with one weeping eye.
A song of mourning for the dead. "With dirge in marriage" = mourning mixed into the wedding.
Sorrow, grief. "Weighing delight and dole."
Shut out or overruled your wiser counsel.
A low or poor estimate. Fortinbras holds "a weak supposal of our worth" — thinks little of us.
Fallen apart and out of order; in disarray.
Allied or joined together. Here, joined with his fantasy of advantage.
To annoy with persistent demands; here, to harass with messages.
Here: concerning, demanding, urging. "Importing the surrender of those lands."
Powerless and bedridden — too feeble to leave his bed.
Here: progress, course, onward movement. "Suppress his further gait" = stop his advance.
Troops raised or conscripted for war.
The detailed, fully spelled-out terms of their instructions.
Let your speed prove your loyalty; let haste recommend your service.
A formal request or petition. "You told us of some suit."
As naturally connected as the head is to the heart — closely and vitally bound.
My dread (greatly revered) lord — a deferential form of address to the king.
Permission and kind approval.
From which place; from where. "From whence I came."
The ceremony of crowning a king.
Forced out of me reluctantly, as if by twisting.
Persistent, hard-working pleading.
To beg or earnestly plead. "I do beseech you."
Here a broad term for any near relative — Claudius calls his nephew Hamlet "cousin."

glossary.term: A little more than kin, and less than kind
glossary.gloss: Hamlet's bitter aside: Claudius is more than a relative (now also stepfather) yet "less than kind" — not truly kindly, and not of Hamlet's own nature.
Literally "in the sunshine," but Hamlet puns on "son": he is too much made a son of the King he despises.
Dark, night-black mourning clothes (and gloomy mood).
Lowered, downcast eyelids; eyes cast down in grief. ("Vail" = to lower.)
Here: ordinary, universal, happening to everyone. The Queen says death is "common"; Hamlet bitterly turns it to mean cheap and vulgar.
I don't deal in mere appearances. Hamlet insists his grief is real, not put on.
A black mourning cloak.
Deep sighing; heavy breathing of grief. "Windy suspiration of forc'd breath."
Behavior, demeanor, bearing. "The dejected haviour of the visage."
The face or its expression.
Goes beyond outward display; cannot be conveyed by appearances. "That within which passeth show."
Outward ornaments or coverings; here, the mere external signs of grief.
The duty a child owes to a parent.
Grief proper to a funeral; dutiful mourning. (From "obsequies," funeral rites — not the modern sense of fawning.)
Grieving, mourning. "Obstinate condolement" = stubborn, excessive grief.
Disrespectful toward God or sacred duty; ungodly. "Impious stubbornness."
Without strength or defense; spiritually weak.
Untrained, uneducated, lacking discipline of mind.
Here: ordinary, common, everyday — not the modern sense of crude. "The most vulgar thing to sense."
Stubborn, irritable resistance.
An exclamation of disgust, shame, or reproach; "shame on it!" or "how disgraceful!"
A corpse; a dead body. "From the first corse till he that died today."
Useless; doing no good; unavailing. "This unprevailing woe."
First in line to inherit the throne; the closest heir.
The German university where Hamlet and Horatio study; a center of new learning (and of Luther). Claudius wants Hamlet to stay home instead of returning.
Contrary to or against our wishes. ("Retrograde" = moving backward, opposed.)
Merry, cheerful. "No jocund health" = no merry toast.
Here: a toast drunk to someone's health.
A full draft of liquor; a deep, celebratory drink (and the carousing around it).
Echo loudly; noise abroad in reply. The heavens will "bruit again" the king's toast.
Hamlet's weary wish that his all-too-solid body would melt away (some texts read "sullied" or "sallied").
God, the eternal one.
God's law (commandment) forbidding suicide. Hamlet laments that this rule keeps him from killing himself.
Worn out, lifeless, and worthless. Hamlet's verdict on the whole world.
A garden gone to ruin, overrun with weeds — Hamlet's image of a corrupt world.
Overgrown, foul, and coarse — things that flourish offensively. ("Rank" = rotten, overgrown.)
A radiant Titan associated with the sun god — a figure of dazzling beauty. Hamlet compares his noble dead father (a Hyperion) to Claudius (a satyr).
A lustful half-goat woodland creature of myth, gross and bestial. Hamlet's contemptuous image of Claudius.
Allow, permit. Old Hamlet would not "beteem" the winds to touch Gertrude's face too roughly.
Hamlet's bitter cry that weakness is the very essence of womankind, prompted by his mother's hasty remarriage.
Before; even before. "Or ere those shoes were old" = before those shoes had worn out.
In Greek myth, a mother whose children were all slain by the gods; she wept endlessly and was turned to weeping stone. "Like Niobe, all tears."
Lacks the power of reasoning. "Wants" = lacks; even a beast without reason would have mourned longer.
The Greek hero of superhuman strength. Hamlet says he is no more like his father than he is like Hercules — i.e., not at all.
Eyes made sore and inflamed by weeping.
Here as a verb: to hurry, rush at speed (like a post-rider). "To post with such dexterity."
A marriage bed considered incestuous — by church law, marrying a dead husband's brother was incest.
A respectful title for a nobleman; "Hail to your lordship" = a greeting to the prince.
Trade titles — Hamlet would rather be Horatio's "friend" than be called "servant."
One who shirks duty or skips school. "A truant disposition" = an idle, school-skipping mood.
Truly; honestly. A mild oath of sincerity.
I pray you; please. A polite, informal request. ("I prithee.")
"Economy!" — Hamlet's sardonic point that the funeral's leftover food was reused ("thriftily") for the wedding feast.
Baked meat pies served at the funeral; reused, Hamlet jokes, at the wedding.
Served up cold; the leftovers stocked the wedding tables.
Bitterest enemy. ("Dearest" here = most intense, not most beloved.)
In my imagination; in my memory's vision — not literally seen.
A fine, admirable, handsome king.
Last night.
Restrain or temper your astonishment. ("Admiration" = wonder, amazement; "season" = moderate.)
An attentive ear; careful listening.

glossary.term: dead waste and middle of the night
glossary.gloss: The empty, deepest hour of midnight.
From head to foot; fully armed in every part. (French: "head to foot.")
Three times.
A military staff or baton carried as a sign of command. "Within his truncheon's length" = an arm's reach away.
Melted nearly to jelly with terror; their courage dissolved by fear.
Prepare or set itself to move (or to speak).
The hinged front of a helmet's visor that covers the face. "He wore his beaver up" = the visor was raised, so his face showed.
The face or its expression. "A countenance more in sorrow than in anger."
Here in a stronger old sense: bewildered, stunned, thrown into confusion.
Count to a hundred. ("Tell" = count, as in a bank teller.)
Streaked with gray. "His beard was grizzled."
Black shot through with silver — the dead king's beard, dark touched with gray. ("Sable" = black.)
Perhaps; maybe.
Assure you; guarantee it. "I warrant you it will."
To open wide. "Though hell itself should gape" = even if hell opened up.
Kept, held fast. "Let it be tenable in your silence" = keep it secret.
To happen by chance. "Whatsoever else shall hap tonight."
To repay or reward. "I will requite your loves."
Between. ("betwixt")
Goodbye; may you do well. (A farewell.)
Treachery; a wrongful or criminal act, especially murder. "I doubt some foul play."
Here often in the old sense: suspect, fear. "I doubt some foul play" = I suspect foul play.
Polonius's gentle daughter, in love with Hamlet; her brother Laertes and father warn her against trusting his courtship.
My luggage and supplies are loaded aboard the ship.
Transport is available; passage is at hand.
The light, playful nature of his affection; Hamlet's love treated as a passing trifle.
A passing whim or impulse of youthful passion. ("Blood" = passion; "toy" = trifle.)
The springtime, the prime of youth. A violet in "primy nature" = a flower of early spring.
A passing pastime; something that fills a single moment and no more.
Growing, increasing. "Nature crescent" = a person still growing.
Muscles; bodily strength and sinews.
As the body ("temple") grows larger. ("Wax" = to grow, increase.)
Along with it; therewith. Often just an emphatic "with."
Deceit, crafty trickery. "No soil nor cautel doth besmirch."
To stain or soil; to dirty.
Choose freely for himself (as if carving his own portion at a feast). A prince cannot, being bound by his rank.
Limited, confined within bounds.
A too-believing, too-trusting ear. "If with too credent ear you list his songs."
Here in two old senses: to listen to ("list his songs"), and to wish or please ("if we list to speak").
A woman's virginity and honor.
Unrestrained, relentless pressing or pestering (here, sexual urging).
Most cautious, most careful (of her reputation). "The chariest maid."
Recklessly generous or wasteful. Even the most careful maid is reckless enough if she merely shows her beauty to the moon.
Blows of slander; attacks of false accusation. ("Calumny" = slander.)
A cankerworm (a destructive caterpillar) eats and ruins. The canker harms young buds before they open.
Here: buds. "Before their buttons be disclos'd" = before the buds open.
Here: opened, unfolded (of a bud or blossom).
Blights; withering, destructive influences. "Contagious blastments."
Hypocritical preachers who don't follow their own teaching.
A person who lives loosely, free of moral restraint, especially sexually.
The easy, pleasure-filled road of flirtation and indulgence — a path that leads to ruin.
Pays no heed to his own advice. ("Reck" = heed; "rede" = counsel, advice.)
The opportunity is favorable; chance grants a happy moment.
An expression of mild rebuke; "shame on you," "how can you delay."
Being waited for; people are waiting on you.
Here as a verb: to write or engrave. "Look thou character" = see that you inscribe these in memory.
Don't blurt out your thoughts; keep your own counsel.
Don't act on any ill-considered, disproportionate thought.

glossary.term: familiar, but by no means vulgar
glossary.gloss: Friendly and approachable, but never cheaply common or over-familiar.
Friends whose loyalty you have tested and proven before taking them in.

glossary.term: Grapple them unto thy soul with hoops of steel
glossary.gloss: Bind tested friends to you as tightly as iron bands hold a barrel.
A brand-new, untested acquaintance (an image of a chick not yet grown feathers).
Here in the old sense: judgment, opinion (not necessarily blame). "Take each man's censure."
Here: clothing, attire. "Costly thy habit as thy purse can buy."
Showy, overly fashionable, gaudy in style.
Tastelessly flashy or overdone. "Rich, not gaudy."
Clothing often reveals a person's character.
Careful management of money or resources; thrift. "Borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry."

glossary.term: to thine own self be true
glossary.gloss: Polonius's famous advice: be honest and consistent with your own nature, and you can't be false to anyone else.
May my blessing ripen and fix this advice in you.
Here: wait, attend. "Your servants tend" = your servants are waiting.
A mild oath of emphasis or surprise; roughly "indeed" or "why." (Originally an oath "by the Virgin Mary.")
Well remembered; good that it's brought to mind.
Generous, freely giving. "Most free and bounteous" — too generous with your time.
Is fitting or proper for; befits. "As it behoves my daughter."
Offers (here, of affection). Polonius then puns on "tender" as money/payment. "Tenders of his affection."
An inexperienced, naive young woman.
Untested, inexperienced. (Not yet "sifted" by hard circumstance.)
Genuine, of true value (as in sterling coin). Polonius warns the "tenders" may not be true currency.

glossary.term: crack the wind of the poor phrase
glossary.gloss: To wear out the word by overusing it (an image of running a horse until it's winded).
Make a fool of me — or present me with a (bastard) baby. A bitter pun by Polonius.
Pressed, urged, begged insistently. "He hath importun'd me with love."
An expression of impatient dismissal or rebuke; "come now," "oh please," "enough of that."
Lent support or credibility to; backed up. "Given countenance to his speech."
Snares set to trap foolish birds. Polonius means Hamlet's vows are traps for a gullible girl. (The woodcock was thought a stupid bird.)

glossary.term: prodigal the soul lends the tongue vows
glossary.gloss: When passion ("the blood") is hot, the heart pours out vows wastefully.
Burned out in both light and heat; the flame dies even as it's promised.
More sparing, less freely available. "Be something scanter of your maiden presence."
Negotiations or interviews; here, granting time and attention to a suitor.
A negotiation or conference, especially with an enemy. (Set your terms higher than a mere command to parley.)
More freedom to roam. A prince may "walk" on a longer leash than Ophelia may.
In short; in brief; to put it briefly.
Go-betweens or agents, here in a shady sense — pimps or panderers. Hamlet's vows are "brokers" luring her on.
Here: garments, clothing. The vows wear holy robes but are not what they seem.
Pleaders begging for sinful ends; agents soliciting unholy desires.
Procurers or pimps; people who arrange illicit sex. The vows breathe like "sanctified and pious bawds."
To deceive or charm into being misled.
Disgrace even a moment of free time — by spending it with Hamlet.
Come along; come with me. ("Ways" = an old emphatic ending.)
Bites sharply; is bitingly cold. ("Shrewdly" = keenly, sharply.)
Biting, sharp, keen air — piercingly cold. ("Eager" = sharp, sour, biting.)
Was accustomed to walk. ("Wont" = habit, custom.)
Cannon, artillery. "Ordnance shot off" = cannon fired.
Drunken revelry and toasting; a carousing party. "Keeps wassail."
A wild, leaping German dance reeled out in drunken revelry.
Gulps of Rhine wine (a German white wine). "Draughts" = drinks, swallows.
A large drum; here part of the noisy fanfare for the king's toasts.
A toast; the drinking of someone's health. "The triumph of his pledge."
"Yes indeed it is." ("Ay" = yes; "marry" = an emphatic oath.)
Born into the custom; raised with it as native habit. (Hamlet says so even though he disapproves of the custom.)

glossary.term: More honour'd in the breach than the observance
glossary.gloss: A custom better broken than kept; one that brings more honor by not following it.
Slandered and blamed. Other nations malign the Danes for their drunkenness.
To call or name. "They clepe us drunkards" = they call us drunkards.
Pig-like, swine-related insults. They smear the Danes with names fit for swine.
Here: one's title, name, or reputation. "Soil our addition" = stain our good name; "the addition of man and country" = the form of address (sir, gentleman, etc.).

glossary.term: pith and marrow of our attribute
glossary.gloss: The essence and core of our reputation; the very heart of what we're credited with.
An inborn flaw or defect of character (an image of an ugly birthmark).
The overgrowth of one dominant temperament or trait. ("Complexion" = one's basic disposition.)
The fences and fortifications of reason. ("Pale" = a fence or boundary.)
Spoils by working through the whole, as too much yeast (leaven) sours dough.
Pleasing, agreeable behavior. ("Plausive" = winning approval.)
Whether a defect is inborn (Nature's uniform) or imposed by chance (one's star/fate).
A tiny amount of bad (a "dram" = a small measure) that taints all the rest.
Angels and agents of God's mercy. "Angels and ministers of grace defend us!"
A wholesome, benevolent spirit (as opposed to a damned goblin).
An evil, hell-bound spirit. Hamlet wonders if the Ghost is good or a devil.
A form that invites questioning; one Hamlet feels he can and must speak to.
Bones buried with proper Christian rites (consecrated in hallowed ground).
Coffined; laid in a tomb or on a bier. "Hearsed in death."
The waxed burial wrappings of a corpse. "Have burst their cerements."
A tomb or burial vault.
Entombed; laid to rest in a grave or urn.
The heavy stone jaws of the tomb (its marble doors imagined as a mouth opening).
Full suit of armor. "In complete steel" = fully armored.
The intermittent moonlight; the night-time world the Ghost revisits.
Mortals baffled and out of their depth before the supernatural.
Here: state of mind, temperament, composure. "Shake our disposition."
Why; for what reason. (Not "where.") "Why is this? Wherefore?"
Something to be imparted or communicated; a message to disclose.
A more secluded, distant spot.
The worth of a pin — i.e., next to nothing. "I do not set my life at a pin's fee."
Juts out and overhangs its base; the cliff overhangs the sea. ("Beetle" = to project, jut over.)
Strip away the rule of your reason; rob you of your sane self-command.
Reckless, despairing impulses (such as the urge to leap). ("Toys" = whims, fancies.)
A unit of depth (about six feet), used for measuring water. "So many fathoms to the sea."
Be guided by us; do as we advise. ("Rul'd" = governed, persuaded.)
Each small blood vessel or sinew. Hamlet's resolve makes every fiber of him as strong as a lion's.
The monstrous lion of Greek myth that Hercules killed; a symbol of fierce, unconquerable strength.
Here in the old sense: hinders or stops me. "Him that lets me" = whoever holds me back.
Let go of me; take your hands off me.
Grows reckless and wild. ("Wax" = to grow.)
Let's go after him; follow!
Here: outcome, result. "To what issue will this come?"

glossary.term: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark
glossary.gloss: Marcellus's famous line: something is deeply corrupt or wrong in Denmark.
To what place; where to. "Whither wilt thou lead me?"
Surrender or give myself up (here, to the torments of purgatory).
Hamlet means "ready and obliged to listen"; the Ghost grimly twists "bound" into "bound to take revenge."
To do penance by burning in flames (an image of purgatory, where sins are purged).

glossary.term: crimes done in my days of nature
glossary.gloss: Sins committed during my mortal life on earth.
Cleansed, purified (by the fires of purgatory).
The place of confinement after death; the Ghost's purgatory whose secrets he may not tell.
Tear up and torment your soul; fill it with horror.
Leap out of their sockets (likening the eyes to stars fixed in heavenly spheres).
Hair lying smoothly together — which terror would make stand on end.
An angry porcupine, with its quills bristling. ("Porpentine" = porcupine.)
A revelation of the eternal world; a proclamation of secrets beyond the grave. ("Blazon" = a formal display or announcement.)
Listen, listen, oh listen! ("List" = listen.)
Ready, quick, well-disposed. "I find thee apt" = you're ready to act.
The bank of Lethe, the mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld; a place of dull oblivion.
Publicly reported; the official story put about. "'Tis given out that..."
A false account or fabricated story. The cause of his death was a lie.
Grossly deceived; foully lied to. ("Rankly" = grossly, offensively.)
A soul that already sensed the truth. Hamlet's "O my prophetic soul!" — he had suspected his uncle.
Adulterous, foul creature. The Ghost's term for Claudius.
The bewitching power of his cleverness. ("Wit" = intelligence, mind.)
Here in its old sense: intelligence, mind, mental sharpness — not humor. "Witchcraft of his wit."
Appearing virtuous; virtuous only in appearance. The Ghost's bitter word for Gertrude.
A decline, defection, falling away. "What a falling off was there" — from a noble husband to a base one.
To glut or satisfy itself fully. "So lust... will sate itself in a celestial bed and prey on garbage."
An hour of carefree, off-guard safety. Claudius struck when old Hamlet felt safe.
A deadly poison (perhaps henbane or yew) that Claudius poured into the sleeping king's ear.
A small bottle or flask (for liquid, here poison).
A distilled poison that causes leprous, scabbing skin. ("Leperous" = leprosy-like.)
Mercury, the fast-flowing liquid metal. "Swift as quicksilver" = as fast as mercury.
To curdle and clot, as milk curdles when soured. The poison curdled his blood.
Sour, acidic drops (like vinegar) that curdle milk. ("Eager" = sour, sharp.)
A scabby rash crusted over ("barked" like tree bark) his skin. ("Tetter" = a skin eruption.)
Like a leper. (A "lazar" = a leper, from Lazarus.)
Here: killed, finished off, made an end of. "At once dispatch'd."
While my sins were in full bloom — killed unconfessed, with sins unforgiven.
Without having received the Eucharist (Holy Communion) before death.
Here: unprepared, not furnished (with last rites); not spiritually equipped for death.
Without having received extreme unction (the last anointing). The king died without any final sacraments.
An accounting (of sins) settled before God. "No reckoning made" = died with sins unconfessed.
Here in its old sense: lust, lechery. "A couch for luxury and damned incest."
Don't corrupt or poison your own soul (in carrying out revenge).
Anything; anything at all. "Nor let thy soul contrive against thy mother aught."
Let God be her judge; don't punish your mother yourself.
A glowing beetle/larva whose light dims at dawn, signaling morning is near.
The morning; daybreak. (Also morning prayer.)
Light that gives no real warmth or effect — the glow-worm paling at dawn.
Goodbye (French, "to God"). The Ghost's farewell: "Adieu, adieu, adieu. Remember me."
Add hell to the list. Hamlet asks if he should call on hell along with heaven and earth.
Tendons, muscles; the body's strength. "You, my sinews, grow not instant old."
Suddenly old; weakened all at once.
Hamlet's troubled, reeling head (the "globe" of his skull) — also a possible nod to the Globe Theatre.
The writing-tablet of the mind; memory imagined as a slate to be wiped clean.
Petty, foolish memories. ("Fond" = foolish, silly.)
Wise sayings or maxims gathered from books. ("Saw" = a proverb, saying.)
Past impressions stamped on the mind.
Lesser, lower, trivial stuff. Hamlet will keep only the Ghost's command, "unmix'd with baser matter."
Deadly, destructive, harmful. "O most pernicious woman!"
A writing tablet or notebook. "My tables" = Hamlet's notebook, in which he writes a memo.
It is fitting; it is proper. ("Meet" = fitting, suitable.)
Latin: "here and everywhere." Hamlet marvels that the Ghost's voice seems to come from all around.
Move to another spot; change position.
Hamlet's wry name for the Ghost, which burrows and speaks from under the stage — "canst work i' th' earth so fast?"
A pioneer — a soldier who digs trenches and mines (tunnels). Hamlet calls the burrowing Ghost "a worthy pioner."
An honest, trustworthy fellow; "good old true coin." Hamlet's affectionate term for the Ghost.
The cellar or space below; here, beneath the stage, where the Ghost's voice comes from.

glossary.term: There are more things in heaven and earth
glossary.gloss: Hamlet's famous line: reality holds far more than human philosophy or science has imagined.
Here: the study of the natural world (what we'd call science and learning), which can't account for the Ghost.
Soever; in whatever way. "How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself."
Think it fitting or proper. ("Meet" = fitting.)
A pretended madness; a grotesque, clownish manner Hamlet plans to put on as a disguise. ("Antic" = grotesque, fantastic.)
Folded or crossed in a knowing way. "With arms encumber'd thus" = arms crossed meaningfully.
A hint or declaration. "Such ambiguous giving out" = such hinting suggestions.
A troubled, restless ghost. "Rest, rest, perturbed spirit."
Offer myself and my goodwill to you; entrust myself to you.
Friendship; friendly help. "My love and friending to you."

glossary.term: The time is out of joint
glossary.gloss: The age is disordered, dislocated, off its hinges — the world has gone wrong, and Hamlet feels cursed to set it right.
Hateful misfortune; a malicious twist of fate. "O cursed spite."
Polonius's servant, sent to Paris to spy on Laertes by spreading rumors and gauging reactions.
Very, extremely wisely. ("Marvellous" used as an intensifier = exceedingly.)
Danes; people from Denmark. Polonius asks which Danes are in Paris.
Where they lodge or dwell. ("Keep" = reside, live.)
Roundabout, circling questioning that gradually gets at the point. ("Drift" = aim, tendency.)
Invented faults; made-up lies. "What forgeries you please" = whatever fictions you like.
Here: gross, foul, excessive. "None so rank as may dishonour him" — no lie so gross.
Be careful; pay attention; watch out.
Unrestrained, loose, undisciplined (especially in pleasure or sex). "Wanton, wild, and usual slips."
Minor faults or lapses; small misdeeds. "Wanton, wild, and usual slips."
Gambling. Listed among the youthful vices a young man might be accused of.
Consorting with prostitutes ("drabs"). The strongest vice Polonius will allow naming.
Soften or temper the accusation; flavor it so it doesn't sound too damning.
Lack of sexual self-control; habitual loose living. Polonius warns against accusing Laertes of this.
Cleverly, skillfully, artfully. "Breathe his faults so quaintly."
The faults that come with youthful freedom; the natural stains of a young man's independence.
The wildness of untamed youthful passion; the unbroken spirit of a young person.
Common to all young men; an impulse that attacks youth generally.
A justified trick or stratagem; a clever, legitimate device. ("Fetch" = a trick, dodge.)
Stains, blemishes. "Slight sullies on my son" = minor smears on his reputation.
The man you want to probe or test. ("Sound" = to test the depth of, to draw out.)
The faults named before; the vices previously mentioned.

glossary.term: closes with you in this consequence
glossary.gloss: Agrees with you and falls in with your lead, replying along these lines.
A mild oath ("by the Catholic Mass"), used for emphasis.
Overcome by his drinking; the worse for drink. ("Rouse" = a bout of carousing.)
Getting into a quarrel during a game of tennis.
A brothel (a "house of sale" of sex). Polonius then defines it: "a brothel, or so forth."
Latin: "namely," "that is to say." Polonius uses it to clarify "a house of sale" — namely, a brothel.

glossary.term: bait of falsehood takes this carp of truth
glossary.gloss: A lie used as bait catches the truth, as an angler's bait lands a fish (a carp).
We who have wisdom and far-reaching cleverness. ("Reach" = mental grasp, capacity.)
Roundabout, indirect methods; circuitous approaches (originally a hunter's detour to come at game).
Indirect attempts; trials by an oblique, curving approach (an image from bowls, where a ball curves on a "bias").
By indirect, roundabout means, discover the straight truth.
"God be with you" — a farewell, the original of "goodbye."
Keep up his music practice; apply himself to his music (here, perhaps with a hint of "keep him busy/observed").
Frightened; terrified. "I have been so affrighted."
A private room; a bedroom. "Sewing in my chamber."
A close-fitting men's jacket of the period, worn over a shirt. Hamlet's is "all unbrac'd" (unfastened), a sign of his disorder.
Unfastened, undone, hanging open. "His doublet all unbrac'd."
Dirty, soiled. "His stockings foul'd."
Fallen down around his ankles like fetters ("gyves" = leg-irons). His ungartered stockings have slipped down.
Pitiful in its meaning or import; a look that seemed to signal great suffering.
A long, intent examination; a careful studying. "Such perusal of my face."
Here: a frenzy or madness; being beside oneself — not joy. "The very ecstasy of love."
Its very nature destroys itself; love's violent quality undoes the lover.
Curse my suspicion! A mild self-rebuke. ("Beshrew" = a curse; "jealousy" = suspicion.)
To overreach in our guesses; to over-calculate, suspecting too much.
Here: observed or noted him closely. ("Quote" = to mark, take note of.)
A former schoolfellow of Hamlet, summoned by the King and Queen to spy on him. Paired with Guildenstern.
A former schoolfellow of Hamlet, summoned with Rosencrantz to spy on him for the King and Queen.
To grant graciously; to be so good as to give. "That you vouchsafe your rest here."
Here: courtesy, good manners befitting gentlefolk. "Show us so much gentry."
To the utmost, completely (an image of a bow drawn fully). "We give up ourselves in the full bent."
A lord or sovereign to whom one owes allegiance; a respectful address to the king. "My good liege."
Here: statecraft, political cunning, scheming. "The trail of policy."
Madness, insanity. (From "luna," the moon, once thought to cause madness.)
Permission to enter; an audience. "Give first admittance to th'ambassadors."
A disturbance of mind or body; a disorder, illness, or upset. "Your son's distemper."
The chief or principal thing. The Queen suspects "the main" is the king's death and her hasty marriage.
An over-hasty, too-soon marriage — Gertrude's quick wedding to Claudius.
Question him closely; examine him to get at the truth. ("Sift" = to scrutinize.)
Deceived; led on with false hopes. Old Norway was "falsely borne in hand" about Fortinbras's aims.
To make a trial or attempt by force of arms; to attack militarily. ("Assay" = attempt, trial.)
Gold coins. "Three thousand crowns in annual fee."
Official authority or orders. "His commission to employ those soldiers."
Peaceful passage; safe transit. Fortinbras asks leave to march his army through Denmark.
Lands and territories under a ruler's control. "Through your dominions."
It pleases us; we approve. ("Like" used impersonally = to please.)
To discuss or reason out at length; to set forth in detail. (Polonius proceeds to do so tediously.)

glossary.term: brevity is the soul of wit
glossary.gloss: Polonius's famous maxim: being brief is the essence of intelligence (ironic, since he is anything but brief). ("Wit" = good sense.)

glossary.term: tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes
glossary.gloss: Long-windedness is mere decorative trimming — the body and ornament, not the substance.
The Queen's request: more substance, less rhetorical fuss. ("Art" = artful, ornate style.)
Here: a figure of speech, a rhetorical device. "A foolish figure."
Consider carefully; weigh this. A pompous word Polonius uses for "pay attention."
To guess or infer. "Now gather, and surmise."
Heavenly; divine. Hamlet's letter calls Ophelia "the celestial... most beautified Ophelia."
Made beautiful, adorned. Polonius scorns it as "a vile phrase" (it could imply artificial, painted beauty).
Poor at writing verse. ("Numbers" = metrical lines, poetry.)
Count or measure my sighs of love (in verse).
This body. Hamlet signs his letter "whilst this machine is to him" = as long as this body is his.
Moreover; in addition. "And more above, hath his solicitings."
Wooings; persistent attempts to win her. "His solicitings."

glossary.term: fell out by time, by means, and place
glossary.gloss: Happened according to the time, manner, and place — i.e., when, how, and where they occurred.
Gladly; willingly. "I would fain prove so" = I'd gladly prove to be so.
In full flight; actively in progress. "This hot love on the wing."
Acted as a silent receptacle; said nothing, like a closed notebook — i.e., kept it secret.
Made my heart turn a blind eye; deliberately overlooked it.
An indifferent, unconcerned eye. "Look'd upon this love with idle sight."
Went straight to the matter; acted plainly and directly.
To address, speak to. "My young mistress thus I did bespeak."
Above your station; beyond your destined rank. Hamlet, a prince, is "out of thy star" for Ophelia.
Here: visiting, frequent coming. "Lock herself from his resort" = keep away from his visits.

glossary.term: took the fruits of my advice
glossary.gloss: Followed and reaped the results of my counsel.
A decline; a falling-off by stages. Hamlet's descent through grief into madness, step by step.
Mourn or lament. "And all we wail for" = and which we all grieve over.
A large hanging tapestry on a wall, big enough to hide behind. Polonius plans to spy from behind one.
Cart drivers; common laborers. Polonius says if he's wrong, he'll quit court and keep a farm with carters.
Approach and accost him at once. ("Board" = to accost; "presently" = immediately.)
Here in its old sense: at once, immediately — not "soon."
"God have mercy" — here used loosely as a thank-you or casual greeting reply.
A seller of fish. Hamlet's odd insult to Polonius; "fishmonger" was also slang for a pimp or bawd.
Rotting flesh the sun kisses (and breeds maggots in). Part of Hamlet's grim, riddling talk about corruption and conception.
Hamlet puns: "conception" means both understanding and becoming pregnant — a blessing, but not the way Ophelia might.
Repeatedly coming back to my daughter. ("Harp on" = dwell insistently on a subject.)
Deeply afflicted; very far into madness. "He is far gone, far gone."
An underlying logic or design in it. Polonius's famous aside: "Though this be madness, yet there is method in't."
Here: full of meaning, apt, sharply pointed. "How pregnant sometimes his replies are."
Here: a felicity of phrase; an apt, lucky turn of speech. "A happiness that often madness hits on."
Quickly arrange or devise. ("Suddenly" = at once; "contrive" = plan.)
Part with; give up. "Anything that I will more willingly part withal."
Tiresome, long-winded old men. Hamlet's mutter about Polonius. ("Tedious" = wearisome.)
Ordinary, middling mortals — neither especially fortunate nor wretched. ("Indifferent" = average, middling.)
The goddess/personification of luck, often pictured with a spinning wheel and as fickle. Rosencrantz and Hamlet trade bawdy jokes about her favors.
Not the topmost favorite of Fortune (not the button on the very top of her cap).
A prostitute; a promiscuous woman. Hamlet calls Fortune "a strumpet" — she gives her favors to anyone.
Enclosures, cells, and prison-pits. Hamlet's image of the world (and Denmark) as a prison.
Confined in a tiny space (a nutshell), yet feeling like a king of infinite space.
By my faith — a mild oath. ("Fay" = faith.)
Class or group you with. "I will not sort you with the rest of my servants."
Wretchedly served; poorly waited on (by bad servants — a bitter joke).
The plain, familiar, well-worn path of friendship; speaking plainly as friends.
Even at a halfpenny, my thanks would be overpriced — a self-deprecating joke about his poverty of spirit.
A visit made of your own free will, not ordered by anyone.
Be honest and fair; deal straight with me.
Earnestly beg or appeal to you (as if by a solemn charm). "Let me conjure you, by the rights of our fellowship."
The harmony and shared bond of our youth together.
I'm watching you; I see through you. ("An eye of" = a watchful eye on.)
Lose nothing, stay perfectly intact (as a bird keeping all its feathers). Their secrecy will be undamaged.
Joy, merriment, gladness. "I have... lost all my mirth."
The earth as a fine, well-made structure — which now seems to Hamlet a barren wasteland.
A barren headland or bare cliff; Hamlet's bleak image of the earth.
An overhanging cover; here the sky imagined as a canopy over the world.
The splendid overarching sky. ("Brave" = fine, splendid; "firmament" = the heavens.)
Adorned (as if with ornamental fretwork) with golden stars. The sky decorated with fire.
A foul, disease-bearing mass of mists. Hamlet's grim view of the once-glorious sky.

glossary.term: What a piece of work is man
glossary.gloss: Hamlet's famous meditation: how marvelous a creation a human being is — noble, godlike — and yet, to him now, mere "dust."
The supreme model or finest example of all living creatures. ("Paragon" = a perfect example.)
The purest essence of mere dust — Hamlet's deflating verdict on humanity for all its glory. ("Quintessence" = the finest distilled essence.)
A meager, sparse reception (as during Lent, a season of fasting). Cold hospitality for the players.
Overtook or passed them on the road. (A hunting term for outstripping the quarry.)
The traveling troupe of professional actors who arrive at Elsinore and will perform Hamlet's "Mousetrap."
A light sword (foil) and a small shield (target) — a knight's stage props.
For free; without payment. The stage-lover won't "sigh gratis" — he'll be paid for his sighs.
The character ruled by a particular "humour" or temperament (e.g. the melancholy or choleric type), a stock stage role.
The comic actor of a troupe; the stage fool whose job is to make the audience laugh.
Easily set off into laughter (an image from a gun's hair-trigger "sere" that fires at a touch).
Unrhymed verse in iambic pentameter — the standard meter of Shakespeare's plays. "The blank verse shall halt for't."
Here: to limp, to stumble in rhythm. The verse will "halt" (go lame) if the lady can't speak freely.
Accustomed; in the habit of. "Those you were wont to take such delight in."
A formal ban or restraint (here, on the actors performing in the city).
A recent upheaval or new development — likely a topical reference to the fashion for boy-actor companies that drew audiences away.
A nestful of child-actors (an "aerie" is an eagle's nest). A troupe of boy players now in fashion.
Young, unfledged hawks; nestlings. A scornful term for the boy-actors who "cry out on the top of question."
Extravagantly applauded; cheered to excess. ("Tyrannically" = outrageously, immoderately.)
To noisily abuse or cry down the ordinary public theaters (and their adult actors).
Gentlemen who wear swords (rapiers) — the fashionable adult playgoers, now mocked by the boy companies.
Pens (made of goose feathers) — standing for the satirical writers behind the boy-actor companies. Gentlemen fear their mockery in print.
Paid for; financially supported. "How are they escoted?" = who funds them?
Continue in the profession of acting. ("The quality" = the acting trade.)
Their future careers as adult actors — which their own current writing mocks.
Egg them on into quarreling. ("Tarre" = to set on, incite, as one sets dogs to fight.)
Came to blows; got into a fistfight. "The poet and the player went to cuffs."
Win; carry off the victory. "Do the boys carry it away?"
Even Hercules and the globe he carried — a likely nod to the Globe Theatre, whose sign showed Hercules bearing the world. The boys outdo even that.
Make scornful faces at him; mock or grimace at him.
Gold coins (of European currency). People now pay fortunes for Claudius's portrait.
A miniature portrait. People who scorned Claudius now buy his little portraits for a fortune.
A strong oath: "God's blood!" Used to express surprise or vehemence. ("'Swounds" = "God's wounds," is similar.)
The proper accompaniment; what belongs with something. "The appurtenance of welcome is fashion and ceremony."

glossary.term: comply with you in this garb
glossary.gloss: Observe the courtesies with you in this manner. ("Garb" = style, fashion of behavior.)
The show of welcome (extended courtesy) I give the players.
Hamlet's grim joke about the tangled family: his uncle is now also his father (stepfather), and his aunt-by-marriage now his mother.
Only mad in one direction, under certain conditions — i.e., not really insane. Hamlet hints his madness is feigned.

glossary.term: know a hawk from a handsaw
glossary.gloss: Can tell quite different things apart — i.e., my wits are sound. ("Handsaw" may be a corruption of "hernshaw," a heron, the hawk's prey.)
Swaddling cloths; the bands wrapped around a newborn baby. Hamlet mocks Polonius as still in his baby-wraps.
A famously great Roman comic actor of antiquity; a byword for the perfect actor. Hamlet teases Polonius with stale news "when Roscius was an actor in Rome."
A dismissive interjection meaning "old news" or "yes, yes, I know." Hamlet brushes off Polonius.
A play observing the strict unity of place (one undivided setting). Part of Polonius's absurd catalogue of dramatic genres.
A play that ignores the classical "unities" and ranges freely. The opposite of "scene individable."
The Roman tragedian whose grave, bloody plays were the model for serious tragedy. "Seneca cannot be too heavy."
The Roman comic playwright, a model for comedy. "Nor Plautus too light."

glossary.term: law of writ and the liberty
glossary.gloss: Both scripted (rule-bound) drama and free, improvised playing — the players excel at both.
A biblical judge of Israel who vowed to sacrifice the first thing he met on returning home — and it was his only daughter. Hamlet calls Polonius "Jephthah" because he too will sacrifice a daughter.
Exceedingly well; surpassingly well. "He loved passing well." ("Passing" = surpassingly.)
A line from the old ballad of Jephthah: "as it fell out by lot, God knows." ("Wot" = knows.)
The religious song or ballad (the ballad of Jephthah). ("Chanson" = song.)
A cutting-short (his interruption) — and a pun on "abridgement" as a pastime/entertainment. The players arrive to cut his talk short.
Fringed with a beard (a "valance" is a fringed drapery). Hamlet jokes the actor's face is now bearded.
To defy or confront me boldly (face to face). A pun: the actor has grown a beard. "Com'st thou to beard me in Denmark?"
A mild oath: "by Our Lady" (the Virgin Mary).
A high, thick-soled platform shoe of the period. The boy who plays women has grown "nearer to heaven" by a chopine's height.
Gold coin no longer accepted as legal currency. A boy's voice "cracked within the ring" (broken) is like a clipped, invalid coin.
A coin cracked past the inner ring is invalid — here, a boy-actor's voice breaking (deepening) so he can no longer play women.
French hawkers, said to fly their hawks at any quarry. "We'll e'en to't like French falconers, fly at anything."
Too refined for the common crowd ("the general" = the general public), who don't appreciate it — like caviar to unrefined tastes.
Spicy or tasty bits; "salads" — here, racy, savory phrases added to make a speech tasty. The play had no such cheap spice.
Accuse ("indict") the author of being affected or pretentious.
In Virgil's Aeneid, the Trojan hero Aeneas tells Queen Dido of Carthage the story of Troy's fall, including Priam's slaughter.
The Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid, who escaped fallen Troy and recounted its destruction to Queen Dido.
Queen of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid, to whom Aeneas tells the tale of Troy's fall.
The aged king of Troy, slaughtered by Pyrrhus during the city's fall. The player's speech describes his death.
The son of Achilles (also called Neoptolemus), a brutal Greek warrior who killed old King Priam during the sack of Troy.
A tiger — Hyrcania (near the Caspian) was famed for its fierce tigers. Pyrrhus is likened to this beast.
Black armor. ("Sable" = black.) Pyrrhus's black-as-night armor matches his dark purpose.
The Trojan Horse, the wooden horse hiding Greek soldiers, by which Troy fell. Pyrrhus lay hidden inside it.
Entirely red. ("Gules" is the heraldic term for red.) Pyrrhus is smeared all over with blood.
Decorated, marked (a heraldry term for sketching arms). Pyrrhus is "horridly trick'd" — grotesquely adorned — with blood.
Caked or crusted, as into a paste. Pyrrhus "bak'd and impasted" with the blood and dust of the burning streets.
Coated over (as with sizing/glue) in clotted blood. ("Coagulate" = clotted; "gore" = blood.)
Glowing red gemstones (or fiery red sores). Pyrrhus's eyes blaze "like carbuncles."
Grandfather; here, an aged man. "Old grandsire Priam."
Soon; presently; in a moment. "Anon he finds him."
Old, ancient sword. Priam's aged blade, too feeble to lift in battle.
Resisting his control; refusing to obey his hand. Priam's sword won't answer his command.
Cruel, deadly sword. ("Fell" = fierce, deadly.)
The strengthless old father (Priam), drained of power. ("Unnerved" = without strength.)
Troy; specifically the citadel or palace of Troy, which collapses in flames as Priam falls.
Drifting clouds high in the sky. "The rack stand still" = the clouds hung motionless.
To tear apart the air/sky. The thunder "doth rend the region."
The one-eyed giant smiths of myth who forged armor for the gods at Vulcan's/Hephaestus's forge. "The Cyclops' hammers."
The Roman god of war. "Mars's armour, forg'd for proof eterne."
Forged to be impenetrable forever. ("Proof" = impenetrable strength; "eterne" = eternal.)
Fortune as a fickle whore who betrays everyone, including the noble. The player curses her.
A formal council or assembly. "All you gods, in general synod" = all the gods in council.
The curved wooden segments of a wheel's rim. "Break all the spokes and fellies from her wheel" — smash Fortune's wheel.
The hub at the center of a wheel. Roll Fortune's wheel-hub down from heaven.
Devils; demons of hell. "As low as to the fiends."
A lively comic song-and-dance performed after a play. Hamlet says Polonius wants "a jig or a tale of bawdry, or he sleeps."
The muffled, veiled queen — Hecuba with her head wrapped in cloth amid Troy's ruin. ("Mobled" = muffled.)
Queen of Troy and Priam's wife, who watched her husband butchered. Her grief becomes Hamlet's measuring-stick for true passion: "What's Hecuba to him?"
Blinding tears. ("Bisson" = blinding; "rheum" = watery discharge, tears.)
A rag or cloth. Hecuba wears a "clout upon that head where late the diadem stood" — a rag where a crown once sat.
A royal crown. "Where late the diadem stood" = where lately the crown had been.
A womb worn out by bearing many children. (Hecuba bore many sons.)
Would have declared (the sight) treason against Fortune; would have denounced Fortune's cruelty.

glossary.term: made milch the burning eyes of heaven
glossary.gloss: Would have made even the stars ("eyes of heaven") weep with milky tears. ("Milch" = milky, tearful.)
Changed color (gone pale) with emotion. Polonius notes the player has "turn'd his colour, and has tears in's eyes."
Lodged, housed, looked after. "See the players well bestowed" = see them well accommodated.

glossary.term: abstracts and brief chronicles of the time
glossary.gloss: Compact summaries and records of the age — the players reflect and report the times. ("Chronicles" = histories.)
An inscription on a tomb honoring the dead. Better a bad epitaph after death than the players' ill report during life.
A mild oath: "by God's little body." An exclamation of mild exasperation.
According to what he deserves. "Use every man after his desert." ("Desert" = what is deserved.)
Escape a whipping; avoid punishment. If everyone got what they deserved, who would escape it?
Generosity; open-handed kindness. "The more merit is in your bounty."
The play-within-the-play the actors will perform; Hamlet will insert lines to mirror his father's murder and "catch the conscience of the King."
A worthless wretch and base coward. Hamlet's furious self-condemnation in his soliloquy.
Here: imagination, a conceived idea or fancy. The player worked himself up to grief from mere "conceit" (imagination).
His face grew pale. ("Wan" = pale.) The actor's face paled with feigned emotion.
All his faculties acting in harmony; his whole being shaped to fit his imagined passion.
Split the ears of everyone present ("the general" = the whole audience) with terrible speech.
Horrify the innocent. ("The free" = those free of guilt; "appal" = to terrify, make pale.)
Dull-spirited, sluggish in temperament. ("Mettle" = spirit; "muddy" = clouded, slow.) Hamlet's self-insult.
To mope, droop, waste away listlessly. "Peak like John-a-dreams."
A nickname for an idle daydreamer who does nothing. Hamlet accuses himself of being such a dreamer.
Not quickened or stirred into action by my cause; barren of purpose, unmoved to act.
Here: destruction, ruin; a foul wrong done. "A damn'd defeat was made" on the king's life.
Cracks my skull ("pate" = head). Hamlet imagines being struck and insulted without retaliating.

glossary.term: gives me the lie i' th' throat
glossary.gloss: Calls me a liar to my very face ("in the throat" = a deep, deliberate insult).
Cowardly, lacking the bitterness for anger. Pigeons were thought to have no bile ("gall"), hence gentle and timid.
To lack the bile that produces anger and bitterness; i.e., to be incapable of resentment. ("Gall" = bile, bitterness.)
The kites (birds of prey) of the sky/region. Hamlet would have fed Claudius's corpse ("offal") to the scavenging kites.
Animal guts and refuse; carrion. Hamlet's contemptuous term for Claudius's flesh.
Lewd, obscene, lecherous. "Bloody, bawdy villain!" — Hamlet's curse on Claudius.
Unnatural, monstrous, without natural feeling. ("Kindless villain" — a villain devoid of kindness and kinship.)
A prostitute; a low woman. Hamlet rages that he merely curses "like a very drab" instead of acting.
The lowest kitchen servant, who scrubs pots. Hamlet despises himself as a foul-mouthed scullion.
An exclamation of disgust; "ugh!" or "phew!" "Fie upon't! Foh!"
Get to work, my mind! Hamlet urges his own brain into action. ("About" = set to it.)
Crimes, evil deeds. Guilty playgoers have confessed their "malefactions" on seeing crimes acted out.
Probe him to the raw, sensitive core (as a surgeon "tents" a wound to search it). Hamlet will probe Claudius's guilt.
To flinch, wince, or start back guiltily. "If he but blench, I know my course."
I'll know what to do; my path will be clear. Hamlet's resolve once he confirms the King's guilt.

glossary.term: the devil hath power t'assume a pleasing shape
glossary.gloss: The devil can disguise himself attractively. Hamlet fears the Ghost may be a demon in his father's likeness, sent to damn him.
More solid, pertinent evidence; firmer proof to act on. ("Relative" = relevant, conclusive.)
Hamlet's plan, summed up: the staged play is the device by which he'll trap the King — "wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King."

glossary.term: catch the conscience of the King
glossary.gloss: Trap the King's guilty conscience — force his guilt to betray itself — by staging a murder like his own.
A roundabout, indirect line of questioning; an attempt to draw something out through hints rather than asking outright.
Assumes, displays, or puts on like a costume. Here: why Hamlet acts so disordered.
Willing to be probed or drawn out. To 'sound' someone is to test their depth, as a sailor sounds the depth of water.
Stays at a wary distance; holds himself apart.
Stingy with conversation; he asked little himself but answered freely.
To test, try, or tempt someone toward something. 'Did you assay him to any pastime?' = did you try to interest him in any amusement.
Overtook; caught up with on the road.
A spur, encouragement, or keenness. 'Give him a further edge' = sharpen his eagerness.
Secretly, privately.
To here; to this place.
To come face to face with, encounter (not 'insult' in this older sense).
Spies; people set to watch in secret.
Position, place, or conceal ourselves.
His usual, customary manner of being.
To give a pretext or plausible cover to something. Reading the book will 'colour' (disguise) Ophelia's being alone.
The outward appearance of piety; a holy-looking face that masks bad intent.
To coat with sweetness; to make something evil look pleasant.
Cosmetics; makeup laid on like plaster. The prostitute's painted cheek.
A speech made up and prettified to hide an ugly truth.
The wounding blows of bad luck, pictured as weapons fired at us by fortune.
Cruel, violent luck or fate that strikes without justice.
A completion or final end; here, a longed-for ending of suffering through death.
The catch, the obstacle, the snag. From lawn bowling, where a 'rub' is anything that knocks the ball off course.
The turmoil and burden of mortal life; the body and its troubles that we 'shuffle off' at death.
A consideration; the reason or regard that makes us hesitate. 'There's the respect / That makes calamity of so long life.'
Insolent, contemptuous treatment; humiliating scorn.
Love that is scorned, unvalued, or not returned.
The arrogant abuse of power by those in official positions.
Contemptuous rejections; humiliating snubs (literally, kicks).

glossary.term: patient merit of the unworthy takes
glossary.gloss: The insults a deserving but patient person has to endure from worthless people.
A final settlement or release; here, putting an end to life as one settles a debt.
A mere dagger; a small pointed blade. Hamlet means one could end life with so simple a tool.
Heavy burdens or loads carried on the back.
Death and whatever lies beyond it, imagined as an unexplored land no one returns from.
A boundary or border; the frontier of the land of death.
The natural healthy color of determination, here drained pale by too much thinking.
Made sickly or sallow, as if covered with the pallor of illness.
The sickly tint that brooding and over-thinking casts over bold purpose.
Great importance and weight; 'pith' is essential strength, 'moment' is significance.
Hush; wait a moment; quiet now.
A beautiful young woman, addressed as if a graceful nature-spirit; Hamlet's term for Ophelia.
Prayers. 'In thy orisons be all my sins remember'd' = remember me in your prayers.
Keepsakes; love-tokens or gifts given as reminders.
To give back, return.
Grow or become poor in worth. 'Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove unkind.'
Chaste, virtuous (of a woman), as well as truthful. Hamlet plays on both senses in 'Are you honest?'
Beautiful. Hamlet pairs it with 'honest' (chaste) to needle Ophelia.
Dealings, exchange, association. 'Better commerce than with honesty' = better company than virtue.
A pimp or madam; one who procures for prostitution. Hamlet says beauty turns chastity into a go-between.
To graft (as onto a plant); virtue grafted onto fallen human nature can't fully overcome it.
The original tree or stem onto which a graft is set; here, sinful human nature.
Have a taste or trace of it. We still 'relish of' our old sinful nature.
A convent — but Elizabethan slang also used it for a brothel, so Hamlet's 'Get thee to a nunnery' bites both ways.
A bearer of children, who are born into sin; Hamlet's bitter view of marriage and childbearing.
Reasonably or moderately virtuous; honest enough, but no saint.
At my command, ready to be summoned; offences he can call up at will.
Out-and-out scoundrels; thorough rascals.
Slander; malicious false accusation. Even the chaste cannot escape it.
The use of cosmetics; women painting their faces. Hamlet attacks female vanity and disguise.
Affected behaviors Hamlet mocks: prancing, mincing along, and using a coy lisping voice.
Lewd, unrestrained behavior; here, women excusing their flirting as innocence.
Overthrown; ruined, cast down. Ophelia mourns Hamlet's 'noble mind' as wrecked.
The mirror of style — the man everyone looked to as the model of how to behave.
The pattern or template of proper conduct; the ideal everyone copied.
The one watched and admired by all who watched; the center of every eye.
Dejected, downcast, wretched.
Youth in full bloom, like a fully opened flower; now blasted (ruined).
Broods or sits like a bird hatching eggs; his melancholy is incubating something dangerous.
Overdue tax or payment owed by England to Denmark; the King's pretext for sending Hamlet away.
Perhaps; by chance.
Blunt and plainspoken with him; direct to the point of sternness.
Lightly, smoothly, and nimbly spoken — Hamlet's advice on delivering lines.
As gladly, as willingly. 'I had as lief' = I would just as soon.
The public announcer who bellowed news in the streets — synonymous with coarse, loud delivery.
To gesture so much with the hands that one seems to saw the air; overacting.
Boisterous, violently loud, blustering.
Wearing a wig (periwig); Hamlet's contempt for a showy, wigged actor.
The cheap-ticket spectators who stood in the pit of the theater, taken to have crude taste.
Silent pantomimed scenes acted out without words.
A ranting, violent god that Christians wrongly imagined Muslims worshipped; a stock blustering character in old plays. To 'overdo Termagant' is to rant outrageously.
Out-rants even Herod — the tyrant of the Nativity who was played as a screaming villain in medieval plays.
The restraint and proportion of real life; the standard acting must not exceed.
An impression or stamp, as a seal leaves in wax; the imprint of the age on the time's 'form'.
Performed weakly, falling short, lagging behind what's required.
Discerning, having good judgment. The opposite of the easily-amused 'unskilful'.
Mere hired apprentice-laborers of Nature, not Nature herself — clumsy makers of badly made men.
Encountered, met with, had to do with. 'As e'er my conversation cop'd withal' = as ever I dealt with.
A sugary, flattering tongue that licks at pompous power for gain.
The readily-bending knee-joints; bowing eagerly to those who can reward you.
Where profit can be gained by flattering; 'thrift' here means gain or success.
Choice; her free choosing. Hamlet's soul 'sealed' Horatio for itself.
Blows, hard knocks. 'Fortune's buffets and rewards' = luck's blows and gifts.
Passion and reason; 'blood' meaning impulse/feeling, 'judgement' meaning cool reason.
A flute that Fortune can play any note on at will — a person ruled by chance and passion.
A person mastered by emotion rather than reason — what Hamlet admires Horatio for not being.
The innermost core of the heart; one's deepest affection.
I pray you; please. A polite, intimate request.
In progress, under way. 'When thou see'st that act a-foot.'
Hidden, concealed guilt. Hamlet watches to see if the King's secret guilt shows itself.
To drive out of hiding, as a fox is forced from its den (kennel).
The forge (stithy = anvil/smithy) of Vulcan, Roman god of fire and metalwork — a place black with soot. Hamlet's imaginings are 'as foul' as it.
Careful, watchful attention.
In judging how he appears and reacts.
To slip anything past unnoticed; to get away with anything.
I must act crazy / play the fool. 'Idle' here means foolish or mad in behavior.
Air — chameleons were thought to live on air. Hamlet says he eats air, 'promise-crammed,' a dig at being fed empty promises about the succession.
Castrated roosters fattened for eating; you can't fatten them on air the way Hamlet is 'fed' on promises.
Roman general and dictator, assassinated in 44 BC; Polonius once played him in a university play, setting up Hamlet's grim pun.
The chief temple-hill of Rome; in popular tradition the place Caesar was killed (actually the Senate's meeting hall).
Marcus Brutus, the friend who joined the plot to stab Caesar; Polonius 'was killed by Brutus' in the old play.
A pun: 'capital' (excellent, also relating to the head/Capitol) and 'calf' (a fool); to kill 'so capital a calf' is a brutish, foolish act.
A more magnetic attraction — Hamlet chooses Ophelia over his mother, playing on 'metal' and a magnet.
A crude double meaning: rural affairs, but with an obscene pun on the first syllable. Hamlet's bawdy needling of Ophelia.
A maker of jigs — the lively comic song-and-dance routines that followed plays. Hamlet sarcastically calls himself the only one who's merry.
A pun: rich dark fur trimmings (luxury) and the black of mourning. Hamlet jokes about dressing finely instead of grieving.
A mild oath, 'by Our Lady' (the Virgin Mary).
A man wearing a wicker horse costume in old May-games and morris dances; suppressed by Puritans, so 'the hobby-horse is forgot' meant a once-loved thing now lost.
Sneaking mischief; secret wrongdoing. 'Miching' = skulking; 'mallecho' (from Spanish) = evil deed.
Probably; most likely.
Signifies or conveys the plot. The 'argument' of a play is its storyline or summary.
To keep a secret. The players 'cannot keep counsel; they'll tell all.'
Wicked, naughty, indecent. 'You are naught' = you're being lewd.
The short motto or rhyme inscribed inside a ring; Hamlet mocks the prologue as that brief.
The chariot of Phoebus (Apollo), the sun-god, which drives the sun across the sky each day.
Roman goddess of the earth; 'Tellus' orbed ground' is the round earth.
Reflected, borrowed light — the moon shines with light borrowed from the sun.
The Greek/Roman god of marriage. 'Hymen did our hands unite' = the god of marriage joined us in wedlock.
Mutual, shared on both sides; reciprocal.
The holy bonds of marriage.
Keeps proportion; women's fear and love stay in step, both either nothing or extreme.
My active, working bodily powers; the strength that keeps me alive, now failing.
A plant proverbial for extreme bitterness; Hamlet hisses it aside, savoring how the Player Queen's words sting his mother.
Low motives of money and material gain, as opposed to true love.
Actions or fulfillments; what passion drives us to do, which destroys itself once the passion cools.
On the slightest chance or trivial cause; grief and joy flip into each other easily.
Forever, for all time. 'This world is not for aye' = the world doesn't last forever.
His favored hangers-on desert him. When the great man falls, his courtiers flee.
Ripens or turns him into an enemy. A false friend tested in need becomes a foe.
Vows or declares more than the truth warrants; overstates her loyalty so insistently it rings false.
A hermit's (anchorite's) meager fare and comfort; the Player Queen wishes herself such bleak confinement if she remarries.
Drains the color/blots out the look of joy; whatever ruins happiness.
Both in this life and the next ('hence' = the hereafter).
Two; the pair of us. 'Never come mischance between us twain.'
Hamlet's mocking title for the play-within-the-play, meant to 'catch the conscience of the King.'
Figuratively, by way of a trope or metaphor — with a pun on 'trap.' Hamlet's slippery answer about the play's title.
The murdered duke in the play-within-the-play; Hamlet names him to needle the King.
The wife of the Duke Gonzago in the inset play.
Roguish, mischievous, villainous. 'A knavish piece of work.'
Souls free of guilt; the innocent, whom the play doesn't touch.
Let the saddle-sore nag flinch — i.e. only the guilty (the chafed horse) will react. 'Jade' = a worn-out horse; 'gall'd' = rubbed raw.
Our shoulders (a horse's withers) aren't chafed — we're not hurt, because we're innocent.
The poisoner in the play-within-the-play, 'nephew to the King' — pointedly echoing Hamlet's own position toward Claudius.
In old drama, the figure who explains the action to the audience; Ophelia calls Hamlet a 'good chorus' for narrating.
Puppets flirting; Hamlet crudely offers to 'interpret' the love-play, as a puppeteer narrates puppets.
Sharp — both witty and cutting/cruel. Ophelia tells Hamlet he is 'keen,' and he turns it bawdy.
Blunt my sharpness — Hamlet twists Ophelia's 'keen' into an obscene joke.
The conspiring moment; the right time, in league with the murderer ('confederate' = allied in a plot).
The curse of Hecate, goddess of witchcraft, the moon, and the underworld; her blessing on poison-weeds.
Three times cursed and poisoned; 'thrice' marks the ritual, magical intensity of the potion.
To seize wrongfully; here the poison's evil powers are to seize and overthrow healthy life.
Still in existence; the (fictional) story of the murder still survives in writing.
A blank gunshot, all flash and no ball; Hamlet taunts that the King is scared of a harmless play.
Stop, leave off, abandon. 'Give o'er the play' = stop the play.
A wounded deer that leaves the herd to weep; Hamlet's image of the guilt-stricken King fleeing.
The unwounded deer that plays on freely — the innocent, untroubled.
To turn renegade, change utterly for the worse, betray one — from the idea of a Christian converting to Islam.
Large rosette ornaments (after Provins roses) worn on fashionable shoes.
Shoes slashed or cut with decorative patterns, in the fashion of the day.
A pack or company of actors ('cry' as of a pack of hounds); Hamlet jokes about earning a share in a troupe.
Legendary model of a perfectly loyal friend (of Damon and Pythias); Hamlet addresses Horatio as such.
Jupiter, king of the Roman gods; Hamlet's symbol of his noble dead father, of whom the realm was 'dismantled.'
A peacock (or a low, base creature) — Hamlet's contemptuous near-rhyme for Claudius instead of 'ass' or 'king.'
A mild oath, 'by God' (French par Dieu); 'indeed, certainly.'
Disturbed, out of sorts, ill in body or mind. The King is 'marvellous distempered.'
Anger; in the old medicine of the four humors, the hot, bilious humor that causes rage.
A medical purge/cleansing; Hamlet jokes that 'curing' the King's anger should be left to the doctor, not him.

glossary.term: put your discourse into some frame
glossary.gloss: Put your talk in order; speak coherently instead of wildly.
A sane, sensible, straightforward reply.
A private chamber or sitting-room (not a clothes cupboard); the Queen's private room where the 'closet scene' takes place.
Before. 'Ere you go to bed' = before you go to bed.
His hands — from the catechism's pledge to keep one's 'hands from picking and stealing.' Hamlet swears by them mockingly.
From the proverb 'while the grass grows, the horse starves' — i.e. waiting for the succession may come too late. Hamlet leaves it 'musty' (stale) and unfinished.
To get to the windward side, as a hunter does to drive game; you're trying to maneuver and trap me.
A net or snare for catching game. 'Drive me into a toil' = herd me into a trap.
The finger-holes of a recorder (flute). Hamlet uses the instrument as a metaphor for being 'played.'
The holes one covers to make notes on a pipe; also the range of feeling someone tries to 'play' in Hamlet.
The full range of an instrument or voice, from lowest to highest note.
A strong oath, 'by God's blood.'
A pun: to vex/annoy, and to press the frets of a stringed instrument. 'You can fret me, but you cannot play upon me.'
Shortly, in a little while (not 'eventually'). Hamlet keeps putting Polonius off with it.

glossary.term: fool me to the top of my bent
glossary.gloss: Push my pretended foolishness as far as it will go; 'bent' is the limit of tension, as of a drawn bow.
The dead of night when witchcraft and evil spirits are abroad; midnight.
Graves seem to open; the imagery of the dead and the supernatural stirring at midnight.
Poisonous infection; hell is imagined breathing out plague into the world.
Roman emperor who murdered his own mother; Hamlet prays not to let 'the soul of Nero' make him kill the Queen.
To use wounding words — to be verbally cruel ('speak daggers to her, but use none').
Rebuked, shamed, scolded. 'How in my words somever she be shent' = however harshly my words shame her.
Howsoever; in whatever way.
The conditions of my royal position/safety. The King can't endure such a threat so near.
Annoyance, harm, injury (a clipped form of 'annoyance').
Welfare, well-being; the prosperity of the king on which many lives depend.
The death or ceasing of a king. 'The cease of majesty / Dies not alone.'
A whirlpool or abyss that sucks down everything near it; the death of a king drags down all around it.
A huge, massive wheel on a mountaintop; an image of the king, whose fall drags down all the lesser parts attached to it.
Fitted and joined together, as a carpenter mortises pieces of wood; the lesser parts locked to the great wheel.
An attached thing; a small appendage joined to something greater.
A violent, crashing downfall.
Chains or shackles for the feet. The King means to chain up ('put fetters on') the danger Hamlet poses.
To rebuke him sharply and to the point; reproach him thoroughly.
Fitting, proper, suitable. ''Tis meet that...' = it's right that...
The words spoken from a position of advantage; conversation overheard to good purpose.
My crime is foul and stinking; 'rank' = grossly corrupt, with a stench reaching to heaven.
The first and oldest curse — God's curse on Cain for murdering his brother Abel; Claudius too killed a brother.
Pulled two ways at once; torn between two purposes so that he does neither.
What is mercy good for, except to face down sin? Claudius reasons about the purpose of God's mercy.
The face of sin; mercy exists to confront wrongdoing.
Prevented beforehand; prayer can keep us from falling into sin before it happens.
The crooked, corrupt ways of this world, where money and influence pervert justice.
A hand full of gold; bribery, which can 'shove by' (push aside) justice.
To push justice aside; to corrupt the law with bribes.
It is not like that in heaven; there can be no bribery or evasion before God.
No dodging, cheating, or sly evasion. In heaven's court one cannot wriggle out of guilt.
A legal phrase: the lawsuit/charge holds. 'There the action lies / In his true nature' = there the case is judged truly.

glossary.term: teeth and forehead of our faults
glossary.gloss: Face to face with our sins in their full reality; forced to confront them openly.
To testify; in heaven we are compelled to bear witness against ourselves.
What remains? What's left to do?
A soul caught like a bird in birdlime (sticky glue smeared to trap birds); the harder it struggles, the more it's stuck.
Make an attempt; try. The King calls on angels to help him try to repent.
Do it conveniently, at exactly the right moment, perfectly timed.
That needs careful examination; that ought to be thought through.
A paid service, a reward — not revenge. Killing Claudius at prayer would send him to heaven, doing him a favor.
In the midst of worldly indulgence and unrepented sin (echoing the sin of Sodom, 'fulness of bread'). Claudius killed Hamlet's father unconfessed.
His sins in full bloom, fully open like flowers; at their ripest.
aliases: broad blown, as flush as May

glossary.gloss: Vigorous and in full bloom, like nature in May; his father died with sins at full strength.
A reckoning, an accounting of the soul before God. 'How his audit stands, who knows save heaven?'
Made ready and fit for the passage of death (into the afterlife); spiritually prepared.
A grasp, seizing, or occasion; here, a more 'horrid hent' is a more dreadful occasion to draw the sword.
Medicine; here, the King's praying is mere medicine that only prolongs his 'sickly days' before death.
To go straight at him; to reprove him bluntly and pointedly.
Unrestrained, excessive, going too far. 'His pranks have been too broad to bear.'
An oath, 'by the cross' (the rood is Christ's cross).
A mirror. Hamlet will set up a 'glass' so the Queen sees the inmost part of herself.
Dead — I'd bet a ducat (a gold coin) on it! Hamlet's cry as he stabs through the arras.
Makes a thrust with the sword (a fencing term).
Hardened it like brass; made the heart brazen and impenetrable.
Armored and fortified against feeling; so hardened it can't feel its own guilt.
Brands it with a mark of shame; a 'blister' was the brand burned on a prostitute or criminal.
The worthless promises of gamblers, sworn lightly and broken easily.
The making of a marriage contract; the solemn bond of marriage, whose very soul is torn out by the Queen's act.
A meaningless string of words; empty babble. Religion's vows reduced to noise.
The solid earth, made of mingled elements; even nature looks sick at the deed.
A sad, sorrowful face. Heaven's own face looks grieved at the act.
As if at the Day of Judgment (Doomsday); the heavens grieve as though the end of the world were at hand.
Roars even in the preface/table of contents; the act is so monstrous it thunders in its mere announcement ('index' = prologue/summary).
A painted portrait or likeness ('counterfeit' = image, 'presentment' = representation) of the two brothers.
The brow/forehead of Jupiter, king of the gods — a face of supreme majesty.
Mercury, the swift winged messenger of the gods, alighting lightly on a hilltop — an image of grace and poise.
Stamped his mark of approval (as a seal authenticates a document); every god seemed to seal Hamlet's father as the model of a man.
A blighted, fungus-rotted ear of grain that infects the healthy ones beside it; Claudius compared to his noble brother.
To feed greedily, gorge, grow fat. 'Batten on this moor' = gorge on this barren wasteland (Claudius).
Barren, boggy wasteland; the worthless ground Hamlet says his mother feeds on, opposed to the 'fair mountain' (his father).
The wild heat and excitement of youthful desire in the blood; at the Queen's age it should be 'tame.'
