Paralyzed, struck dumb as by a stroke (apoplexy); her senses must be deadened to choose so wrongly.
Enslaved, held in thrall. Even madness was never so enslaved to delusion as to make her choice.
Cheated you at blind man's bluff ('hoodman-blind') — some devil tricked you while your eyes were covered.
Without (from French). 'Smelling sans all' = the sense of smell without all the others.
To be dazed, stupefied, dull-witted. Even a single failing sense couldn't be so witless as the Queen.
To mutiny, rebel. 'If thou canst mutine in a matron's bones' = if hell can stir rebellion even in a middle-aged woman.
A mature married woman; the Queen, past youth, in whom such lust should be quenched.
Overpowering, driving passion or desire that 'gives the charge' (sounds the attack).
Reason acts as a pimp ('panders') for desire, serving lust instead of restraining it.
Dyed-in, ingrained stains that won't wash out; the indelible black spots the Queen sees on her own soul.
Lose their dye/color; the soul's stains 'will not leave their tinct' = won't fade out.
A bed greasy with sweat and lust; foul and corrupt ('enseamed' = soaked in grease/filth).
A pigpen; Hamlet's disgusted image of the Queen and Claudius 'honeying' over the 'nasty sty.'
A tenth part; 'not the twentieth part the tithe' = not even a fraction of a fraction of the worth of your former husband.
Your previous husband (Hamlet's father); 'precedent' = former, earlier.
A clownish villain among kings — 'the Vice' was the comic devil-figure of old morality plays; Claudius is a mockery of a king.
A thief/pickpocket of the kingdom — Claudius stole the crown like a common cutpurse stealing a purse.
A patchwork figure, like a fool's motley costume; a king made of scraps, no real king at all.
To sharpen, as on a whetstone. The Ghost comes to 'whet' Hamlet's dulled resolve.
Empty air, nothingness. The Queen sees Hamlet stare at empty space ('bend your eye on vacancy').
The bodiless, invisible air; the Queen marvels that Hamlet talks to nothing.
Hairs lying flat in place; in terror they 'start up and stand an end' (stand on end).
As if there were life in lifeless outgrowths — hair and nails ('excrements') were thought dead matter, yet his rise as if alive.
His shape (the Ghost) together with the reason for his coming; the sight would move even stones.
Capable of feeling; the Ghost's plea could make even stones 'capable' (responsive, full of feeling).
Turn aside my stern purpose; the piteous sight risks softening Hamlet's resolve to act.
Lack the right character/justification; what Hamlet does will lose its proper color (he'll weep instead of shedding blood).

glossary.term: in his habit as he liv’d
glossary.gloss: Dressed in the clothes he wore when alive; the Ghost appears in his familiar garments.
aliases: in his habit as he liv'd

glossary.gloss: A doorway, gateway. The Ghost goes out 'at the portal.'
A mere invention of the mind, like counterfeit coin; the Queen says the Ghost is something Hamlet's mind minted.
A shape with no body; a hallucination, which 'ecstasy' (madness) is skilled at producing.
To repeat word for word; Hamlet offers to recite his words again to prove he's not mad.
To leap or skip away from; madness would 'gambol from' (jump erratically off) such a coherent account.
A soothing, deceptive ointment; the comforting lie. 'Lay not that flattering unction to your soul.'
To cover over with a thin skin; the comforting lie only films over the wound while corruption festers beneath.
A festering sore; the Queen's guilt, which will keep rotting if merely covered over.
Undermining and eating away from inside, like a sapper digging beneath a wall ('mining').
Don't fertilize the weeds — don't feed your sins to make them grow ('ranker') by excusing them.
More foul, more grossly overgrown; weeds (sins) made worse by 'manuring' them.
Bloated, flabby, corrupt times. 'The fatness of these pursy times' = our overfed, decadent age.
To bow ('curb') and beg permission; in a corrupt age, virtue itself has to grovel to do good.
Split my heart in two; the Queen's cry that Hamlet's words have broken her heart.
Put on virtue, act it even if you don't yet feel it — Hamlet's advice that practicing goodness can become real.
Habit, personified as a monster that dulls all feeling but can also, by repetition, build good habits.
A garment or uniform ('livery' = a servant's outfit); habit clothes good actions in an easily-worn form.
The imprint of inborn character; habit 'almost can change the stamp of nature' — even reshape what seems fixed.
God's whip and agent of punishment; Hamlet sees himself appointed to punish (and be punished for) the deed.
To dispose of / put away the body. Hamlet will 'bestow' (deal with) Polonius's corpse.
Harsh now in order to do good in the end; severity meant for her ultimate benefit.
The bloated, swollen King — Claudius, fat with drink and indulgence; Hamlet's contemptuous term.
A pet endearment used between lovers; Hamlet sneers at Claudius calling the Queen his 'mouse.'
Foul, sweaty, smoky kisses ('reechy' = grimy, rank).
Fondling or pawing at your neck with his fingers; Hamlet's revolted image of Claudius's caresses.
To unravel and reveal the whole secret; tease out the truth that Hamlet is only feigning madness.
Mad only as a deliberate ploy; pretending madness on purpose, not truly insane.
A toad; one of Hamlet's loathsome names for Claudius.
A tomcat; an old, foul tom — another of Hamlet's contemptuous names for Claudius.
Matters of deep, intimate importance; serious secrets a queen shouldn't reveal to such creatures.

glossary.term: in despite of sense and secrecy
glossary.gloss: In defiance of all good sense and the need for secrecy; recklessly giving the secret away.
To make an experiment, test what happens — like the famous ape who climbed into the basket to find out.
Venomous snakes with fangs intact; Hamlet trusts his schoolfellows as little as deadly snakes.
An official command or order; the sealed orders Rosencrantz and Guildenstern carry.
To escort/lead me toward villainy or treachery; they're conducting Hamlet into a trap.
A military engineer who builds bombs and mines ('engines' of war); destined to be blown up by his own device.
Blown up by his own bomb. A 'petard' was a small explosive charge; the saboteur is destroyed by the very weapon he set.

glossary.term: delve one yard below their mines
glossary.gloss: To dig (counter-mine) a yard beneath the enemy's tunnels, so as to blow up their explosives from below; Hamlet will outmaneuver them.
Sets me moving/scheming in a hurry (with a pun on packing up to leave for England, and packing off the corpse).
To drag the body. Hamlet's brutally plain way of saying he'll haul Polonius's corpse away.
Chattering, babbling foolishly. The dead Polonius 'was in life a foolish prating knave.'
A royal adviser; here, the dead Polonius, ironically now 'most still, most secret, and most grave.'
A long, slender thrusting sword, the fashionable dueling weapon. It is Hamlet's and Laertes's weapon in the final fencing match.
A wild, headstrong fit of imagination. The Queen's phrase for the crazed impulse in which Hamlet killed Polonius.
Foresight; careful management of what is to come. The King says his own foresight should have kept the dangerous Hamlet under control.
Away from people, out of company. The King wishes he had kept the mad Hamlet isolated.
Becoming known, being made public. The King compares hiding Hamlet's madness to a man concealing a shameful disease so it won't be revealed.
The essential core or vital center of something. The disease, kept hidden, feeds on the very pith (the marrow) of life.
A reply or answer. Hamlet sneers that a king's son owes no real answer to a 'sponge' like Rosencrantz.
A gathering, like a formal assembly or council, of scheming worms. Hamlet's grim joke that Polonius is 'at supper' being eaten by worms.
Different courses of the same meal. Hamlet says a fat king and a lean beggar are just two dishes served at one table for the worms.
To make a royal journey or state tour. Hamlet jokes a king can 'go a progress' through a beggar's guts after being eaten by a worm a fish ate.
To smell out, to detect by smell. The King will 'nose' the rotting Polonius on the stairs to the lobby.
To regard with care; to value and look after. The King claims he tenders (cares deeply for) Hamlet's safety.
A sailing ship. The bark is ready to carry Hamlet to England.
An angel, traditionally one with special knowledge. Hamlet hints he sees through the King's plot, as a cherub sees the King's true purposes.
A scar from a healed wound. England's scar from the Danish sword is still raw, so it owes Denmark obedience.
Willing fear or respect freely given. England pays homage to Denmark out of this awe.
A royal command or official order. The King's sealed letters carry the sovereign process demanding Hamlet's death.
A persistent feverish heat in the blood (a wasting fever). Hamlet rages in the King's blood like a fever that must be cured.
Armed forces; troops. Hamlet asks the Captain whose 'powers' (whose army) these are.
Owned outright as property. The land wouldn't fetch a higher price even if sold in fee (sold absolutely).
A Pole; the Polish people or king. Hamlet predicts the Polack will not bother to defend such worthless ground.
An abscess or festering swelling. The pointless war is the inward abscess of too much wealth and peace, that bursts unseen.
The power of reasoning; the capacity to think things through. Hamlet says God gave humans 'large discourse,' looking before and after, not to leave it unused.
To grow stale or moldy from disuse. Hamlet condemns letting his god-given reason 'fust' (rot) within him.
A cowardly hesitation or doubt. Hamlet wonders if his inaction comes from a craven scruple about thinking too carefully.
As plain and obvious as the ground itself. Examples 'gross as earth' urge Hamlet to act.

glossary.term: makes mouths at the invisible event
glossary.gloss: Defiantly mocks the unknown outcome. Fortinbras's spirit scorns whatever fate may come.
Persistently demanding, refusing to be put off. The mad Ophelia is importunate to be let in to the Queen.
Driven out of one's mind; deranged. Ophelia is described as 'distract' (mad with grief).
Kicks angrily at trifles. The mad Ophelia takes offense at the smallest things.
An attempt to gather meaning; inference. Ophelia's broken speech moves hearers to 'collection,' guessing at her sense.
A trifle; a small worthless thing. To the guilty Queen, every little thing seems the prelude to some disaster.
A misfortune or calamity (used as a noun here). Each trifle seems a prologue to some great amiss.
A hat bearing a cockle (scallop) shell, the badge of a pilgrim to a holy shrine. In Ophelia's song, a true love is known by his pilgrim's hat, staff, and sandals.
An old plural of 'shoe.' The pilgrim wears 'sandal shoon' (sandal shoes) in Ophelia's song.
Garnished or strewn (literally, dotted with strips of fat for cooking). The shroud in Ophelia's song is larded all with sweet flowers.
'God yield (reward) you' — a thank-you blessing. Ophelia, in her madness, blesses the King.

glossary.term: the owl was a baker's daughter
glossary.gloss: A folk legend in which a baker's daughter was turned into an owl for refusing Christ bread. Ophelia cites it to mean we cannot know what we may become.
February 14, by tradition the day the first girl a man saw became his valentine. Ophelia's bawdy song uses the custom for a tale of seduction.
Early; in good time. In the song the maid comes to the window early in the morning.
Opened (a contraction of 'did up'). The young man dupp'd (opened) the chamber door.
A mild oath, 'by Jesus.' Ophelia swears 'By Gis and by Saint Charity' in her song.
A mild oath, 'by God' (a deliberately coarse-sounding euphemism). Ophelia uses it in her bawdy song.
Secrecy and disorderly haste. The King admits Polonius was buried hastily and in secret ('in hugger-mugger').
To bury in the ground. They acted clumsily ('greenly') in hurrying to inter Polonius.
Whispering gossips or rumor-mongers. Laertes lacks no buzzers to poison his ear against the King.
To accuse formally; to put on trial. Rumor will not hesitate to arraign the King for the death.
A cannon loaded with scattering shot, hitting many targets at once. The King's griefs strike him like a murdering piece, in many places.
Swiss mercenary guards, who commonly served as royal bodyguards. The King calls for his Switzers to guard the door.
Rising above and looking over its boundary. The ocean overpeering its shore-limit describes Laertes's flooding rebellion.
A rebellious armed band or uprising. Laertes storms the castle 'in a riotous head' of followers.
Overpowers your officers and authority. Laertes's mob sweeps aside the King's guards.
A disorderly crowd of common people. The rabble cheers for Laertes as king.
A hunting term for following a scent backward, the wrong way. The Queen scolds the mob as hounds running 'counter' on a false trail.
A man whose wife is unfaithful, a figure of shame and mockery. Laertes says any calm blood in him would brand his father a cuckold and his mother a harlot.
To surround and protect a king like a protective fence. Such divinity 'doth hedge a king' that treason can do little.
Tricked or deceived, as by a conjurer's sleight of hand. Laertes vows he will not be juggled with about his father's death.
Sweeping in all the stakes at once, friend and foe alike. The King asks if Laertes's revenge will indiscriminately take everyone.
A bird believed to feed its young with blood from its own breast, a symbol of self-sacrifice. Laertes vows to nourish his father's true friends with his own blood.
Keenly, with deep feeling. The King insists he is most sensibly grieved by Polonius's death.
A figure of fresh young beauty in bloom. Laertes laments the mad Ophelia as his lost 'rose of May.'
A lesson or instruction (its older sense). Laertes calls Ophelia's flower-talk 'a document in madness,' a lesson taught even in her ravings.
A fragrant herb traditionally symbolizing remembrance and used at funerals and weddings. Ophelia gives it 'for remembrance.'
A flower whose name comes from French pensees, 'thoughts.' Ophelia gives them 'for thoughts.'
An herb symbolizing flattery and, with columbines, marital infidelity. Ophelia distributes it among her mad flower-gifts.
Flowers symbolizing ingratitude and unfaithfulness in love (and the cuckold's horns). Ophelia hands them out in her madness.
A bitter herb symbolizing sorrow and repentance, also called 'herb of grace.' Ophelia keeps some for herself and bids it be worn 'with a difference.'
Another name for rue, linked to repentance because it was used to sprinkle holy water. Ophelia notes rue may be called this on Sundays.
A heraldic phrase for a mark added to a coat of arms to distinguish one bearer from another. Ophelia tells the Queen to wear her rue (sorrow) 'with a difference,' for a different reason.
A flower symbolizing innocence or unhappy love. Ophelia offers a daisy among her mad gifts.
Flowers symbolizing faithfulness, which Ophelia says all withered when her father died.
The refrain of a popular old love song. The mad Ophelia sings this snatch about 'sweet Robin' being all her joy.
An indirect involvement, as opposed to a direct one. The King offers his crown if found guilty by direct or collateral hand in the death.
A diamond-shaped tablet bearing a dead nobleman's coat of arms, hung up at a funeral. Laertes laments his father had no hatchment over his bones.
A formal public ceremony or display. Polonius's burial lacked the noble rite and formal ostentation due him.
Let the punishment (originally an executioner's axe) strike where the guilt lies. The King promises Laertes justice.
Hamlet's own ironic title for himself as he was being sent to England. The pirate letter says it comes from 'the ambassador that was bound for England.'
Equipment and outfitting. The attacking pirate ship was 'of very warlike appointment' (well-armed).
Courage forced on one by necessity. Too slow to flee, Hamlet's crew 'put on a compelled valour' and fought.
Merciful thieves; pirates who spared their captive expecting a favor in return. They dealt with Hamlet like 'thieves of mercy.'
A formal release from blame or debt. The King says his innocence is now sealed in Laertes's conscience like an acquittance.
Deserving the death penalty. The crimes against the King were 'so crimeful and so capital in nature.'
Weak; lacking force or muscle. The King admits his reasons may seem unsinew'd (feeble) to Laertes.
Closely joined, bound together. The Queen is so 'conjunctive' to the King's life and soul that he cannot move without her.
The common people; the public at large. The great love the 'general gender' bear Hamlet is the King's other reason for not striking openly.
Shackles or fetters for the legs. The people's affection would turn Hamlet's gyves (his crimes) into graces.
Made with too light a shaft. The King's arrows (his accusations), too slightly timbered for the strong wind of popular love, would blow back on him.
Spiritless and sluggish. The King insists he is not made of stuff so flat and dull as to ignore danger.
Turning aside from his journey (a falconry term: a hawk 'checks' when it abandons its quarry for other prey). The King supposes Hamlet has 'checked' at his voyage and returned.
The instrument or agent through which something is done. Laertes wants to be 'the organ' of Hamlet's death.
Rank or standing (literally, a seat). The skill Hamlet envied was, in the King's view, of the unworthiest siege (lowest rank).
A ribbon, here an ornament of youth. The admired skill is 'a very riband in the cap of youth,' a fitting decoration.
Dark, dignified garments suited to old age. Settled age suits its sables (dark furs) and weeds (grave clothing).
A celebrated Norman gentleman and master horseman, praised by the King as 'the brooch and gem of all the nation.' His report of Laertes's swordsmanship stirred Hamlet's envy.
Fencers; skilled swordsmen (from French escrimeur). Lamord swore the scrimers of France were nothing against Laertes.
To poison, here figuratively with envy. Lamord's praise so envenomed Hamlet with envy that he longed to fence with Laertes.
An excess or overgrowth (here meaning a fullness, by association with the inflammation). The King warns that goodness grown to a pleurisy dies of its own too-much.
A sigh thought to drain the heart's blood, thus wasteful of life. A delayed 'should' is like such a sigh, that 'hurts by easing.'
To shelter or give sanctuary to. The King agrees no place, not even a church, should sanctuarize a murderer from revenge.
Light, blunted fencing swords used for practice. The plot relies on Laertes secretly choosing an unblunted, poisoned blade among the foils.
Not blunted; with a sharp, lethal point. Laertes is to choose a 'sword unbated' to wound Hamlet for real.
A treacherous thrust disguised as a practice move. Laertes will kill Hamlet with a pass of practice.
An ointment or salve; here a deadly poison to smear on the blade. Laertes bought a mortal unction from a quack.
A traveling quack who sold dubious medicines from a platform. Laertes bought his poison from a mountebank.
A medicinal poultice or plaster laid on a wound. No cataplasm, however rare, could cure a scratch from the poisoned blade.
Medicinal herbs; plants used singly as remedies. No medicine from all the simples with healing virtue can save the poisoned man.
To graze or wound the skin. If Laertes can gall Hamlet even slightly with the poison, it may be fatal.
A cup prepared for this special occasion. The King will ready a poisoned chalice in case the blade fails.
A thrust or stab in fencing (from Italian stoccata). If Hamlet escapes Laertes's venomed stuck, the poisoned drink will get him.
A tree associated with grief and forsaken love, growing beside the brook where Ophelia drowned.
A wildflower (likely the ragged-robin) used in Ophelia's funeral garland. One of the blossoms she wove before drowning.
A wild orchid with suggestive roots, which shepherds gave a coarse name and chaste maids called 'dead men's fingers.' Part of Ophelia's drowning garland.
The prim country name for the wild orchid called 'long purples,' from its pale finger-like roots. Used in Ophelia's fatal garland.
Garlands of flowers and plants woven into a crown. Ophelia was hanging her coronet weeds on the willow when the branch broke.
Unaware; not taking in. As she floated, Ophelia seemed 'incapable of her own distress,' senseless to her danger.
A song or melody. Her water-soaked clothes pulled Ophelia from her melodious lay to muddy death.
Rustic comic characters; here the two gravediggers whose joking opens Act V. The 'First Clown' digs Ophelia's grave and unearths Yorick's skull.
Burial in consecrated ground with church rites, denied to suicides. The gravediggers debate whether the apparent suicide Ophelia deserves it.
A coroner, the official who held an inquest on a sudden death. The crowner 'sat on' Ophelia and ruled it Christian burial.
The gravedigger's comic blunder for 'se defendendo' (in self-defense), the legal excuse for a justified death. He garbles the law in arguing about Ophelia's drowning.
The gravedigger's mangled version of Latin 'ergo,' meaning 'therefore.' He uses it to cap his nonsense logic.
'Good fellow digger' — a homely form of address. One gravedigger calls the other 'goodman delver' (a delver is one who digs).
Whether he wants to or not (the origin of 'willy-nilly'). The gravedigger argues a man who goes to the water drowns himself willy-nilly.
The law as applied at a coroner's inquest ('quest' = inquest). The gravedigger insists his reasoning is genuine crowner's quest law.
Fellow Christians; one's equals in the faith. The gravedigger grumbles that great folk may drown themselves more freely than their 'even Christian.'
Both 'carried weapons' and 'had a coat of arms' (the mark of a gentleman). The gravedigger's pun: Adam 'bore arms' because he dug with his arms.
To stop work, as oxen are unyoked at day's end. The gravedigger tells his mate to give the answer and then 'unyoke,' quit.
A mild oath, 'by the Mass.' The Second Clown exclaims it when he gives up on the riddle.
Beat or rack your brains; strain to think. The gravedigger tells his mate to cudgel his brains no further.
Apparently the name of a nearby alehouse keeper. The gravedigger sends his mate to Yaughan to fetch liquor.
A drinking vessel or tankard; a large measure of liquor. The gravedigger wants a stoup of liquor fetched.
Benefit or advantage. In the gravedigger's song, love was sweet 'for my behove' (for my good).
Dashes or knocks (one thing against another). Hamlet notes how the gravedigger jowls the skull to the ground.
The bone with which Cain, in tradition, slew his brother Abel — the first murder. Hamlet imagines the tossed skull as Cain's murderous jawbone.
The head or skull. Hamlet wonders if the skull was the 'pate of a politician.'
Lords it over; treats with contempt as a superior would. The lowly gravedigger now o'er-offices the skull of a once-scheming politician.
'Good morning'; a courteous greeting. Hamlet imitates a fawning courtier's 'Good morrow, sweet lord.'
A slang word for the head or skull. The skull is knocked about the mazard with a sexton's spade.
A church officer who dug graves and rang bells. The skull is struck with a sexton's spade; the gravedigger has been sexton thirty years.
An old game in which pieces of wood were thrown at a stake. Hamlet is sickened that bones are tossed about as if to play loggets.
Fine legal quibbles; hairsplitting subtleties. Hamlet mocks a dead lawyer's quiddits, now useless.
Petty legal tricks or evasions. Like 'quiddits,' the lawyer's quillets cannot save him now.
Legal terms of holding land. Among the dead lawyer's lost cunning are his tenures.
Slang for the head or skull. The lawyer's skull is knocked about the sconce with a dirty shovel.
A lawsuit for being physically struck. Hamlet jokes the dead lawyer can't even sue for the blows to his skull.
Legal bonds securing a debt against land. Part of the dead lawyer's now-worthless paperwork.
Legal bonds acknowledging a debt or obligation. Another of the lawyer's useless legal instruments.
Legal devices used to guarantee secure title to land. Hamlet lists them among the dead buyer-of-land's vain documents.
A legal procedure for securing full ownership of land. Hamlet puns: the recovery of his recoveries is a head full of dirt.
Both a legal mode of conveying land and 'the end.' Hamlet puns: 'Is this the fine of his fines?' — the end of all his legal fines.
Legal contracts (so called because their edges were notched to match). A man's whole estate scarcely fills a coffin the size of a pair of indentures.
Legal documents transferring property. All the dead man's conveyances will scarcely fit in his grave.
The living. Hamlet jokes the grave is for the dead, not the quick.
Precise; insistent on exact meaning. Hamlet marvels how 'absolute the knave is,' splitting words so finely.
Exactly, by the precise rule (as a compass-card marks every point). One must speak 'by the card' or the gravedigger's word-twisting will undo you.
Deliberate ambiguity; using words in a double sense to mislead. The gravedigger's equivocation traps Hamlet.
Refined, over-fastidious; affectedly precise. Hamlet says the age has grown so 'picked' that peasant treads on courtier's heel.
A chilblain or chapped sore on the heel. The peasant follows so close he galls (rubs) the courtier's kibe.
Corpses rotten with disease (especially the pox). The gravedigger notes many pocky corses now barely survive burial.
A worker who cures animal hides into leather. A tanner's body, the gravedigger jokes, lasts longest because his trade tans his own skin.
Literally 'son of a whore,' used as a coarse intensifier like 'damned' or 'wretched.' The gravedigger calls water a 'whoreson decayer' of dead bodies.
White wine from the Rhine region of Germany. The gravedigger recalls Yorick once poured a flagon of Rhenish on his head.
The dead court jester whose skull the gravedigger unearths. Hamlet, who loved him as a boy, holds the skull and meditates on death and decay.
A court fool kept to entertain the king with wit and antics. Yorick was 'the King's jester.'
The throat or stomach contents; what rises when one feels sick. Hamlet's 'gorge rises' in disgust at the skull.
Taunts; mocking jokes. Hamlet asks where Yorick's gibes are now.
Playful leaps and antics. Where now, Hamlet asks, are Yorick's gambols?
Both 'with the lower jaw (chop) missing' and 'crestfallen, downcast.' Hamlet's grim pun on the jawless skull.
The face or appearance. To this 'favour' (this skull-face) even a painted lady must come.
Alexander the Great, conqueror of the ancient world. Hamlet imagines even his noble dust ending up plugging a bunghole.
The stopper-hole of a barrel. Hamlet traces mighty Alexander's dust to stopping a bung-hole.
Too minutely; with excessive care. Horatio says it would be considering 'too curiously' to trace Alexander's dust so far.
A mixture of clay and earth used in building. Of earth we make loam, and loam may patch a wall.
The mighty Julius Caesar. Hamlet's verse: even Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might stop a hole to keep the wind out.
Incomplete or curtailed funeral ceremonies. Ophelia's burial has 'maimed rites,' betraying a suspected suicide.
To destroy or do away with. The funeral's stinted rites show the corpse 'did with desperate hand fordo it own life' (took its own life).
Of high rank or social standing. The maimed rites suggest the dead person was 'of some estate.'
Let us crouch down and hide. Hamlet tells Horatio to 'couch we awhile' and watch the funeral unseen.
Funeral rites and ceremonies. Ophelia's obsequies are enlarged as far as the doubtful circumstances allow.
Authorizations; what is officially permitted. The priest enlarged Ophelia's rites as far as their 'warranties' allowed.
Unconsecrated; not blessed ground. Without royal command, Ophelia would have lain in unsanctified ground as a suicide.
The trumpet sounding on Judgment Day to raise the dead. A suicide would lie in unhallowed ground till the last trumpet.
Broken bits of pottery. By rights, shards, flints, and pebbles should be thrown on a suicide's grave instead of prayers.
Flowers strewn on a grave. Ophelia is allowed her 'maiden strewments,' the flowers due a virgin.
A solemn sung mass for the dead. The priest refuses to sing a 'sage requiem' over the doubtful death.
Souls that died peacefully at peace with God. A full requiem belongs to peace-parted souls, not to a possible suicide.
An attending, serving angel in heaven. Laertes vows his sister will be a ministering angel while the priest lies howling in hell.
A mountain in Greek myth that giants piled on others to assault heaven. Laertes wants Ophelia's grave heaped higher than old Pelion.
The towering mountain home of the Greek gods. Laertes wishes the grave-mound to overtop blue Olympus.
The planets, which seem to wander against the fixed stars. Hamlet's grief, he boasts, conjures even the wandering stars to stand still.
Hamlet's proclamation of himself as the rightful prince of Denmark ('the Dane' meaning its royal head). He announces it leaping into Ophelia's grave.
Hot-tempered, quick to anger (the spleen was thought the seat of temper). Hamlet warns he is not splenative, yet has something dangerous in him.
A violent oath, contracted from 'God's wounds.' Hamlet swears it, daring Laertes to match his grief.
Vinegar (a bitter drink). Hamlet challenges Laertes: will he drink up eisel, eat a crocodile, to prove his love?
To talk on idly or boastfully. If Laertes will 'prate of mountains,' Hamlet will outdo him.
The torrid zone of the sky near the sun. Hamlet imagines a grave-mound piled so high it singes its top against the burning zone.
A Greek mountain piled by giants on Pelion to reach heaven. Hamlet vows to make Ossa look like a wart beside the mound he'd raise.
A dove's pair of newly hatched, golden-downed chicks. As a dove broods quietly when her couplets hatch, so Hamlet's fit will subside into silence.
An immediate test or trial of strength. The King urges putting the matter to the present push.
Iron shackles that confined a prisoner's feet, used aboard ship. Hamlet lay worse than mutineers in the bilboes.
To shape roughly, leaving the finishing to another (here, to providence). A divinity shapes our ends, however we rough-hew them.
A coarse, short-skirted coat worn at sea. Hamlet wrapped his sea-gown about him as he crept in the dark.
Stole; took with the fingers, pilfered. Hamlet 'finger'd their packet,' the sealed orders.
The King's official sealed order. Opening it, Hamlet found the command for his own execution.
Bogeymen and terrors; imaginary dangers used as a pretext. The order cited such bugs and goblins in Hamlet's life as reason to kill him.
The reading-over of a document. On the very supervise of the order, with no delay, Hamlet's head was to be struck off.
Statesmen; men of political affairs. Hamlet once thought, like our statists, that writing a fair hand was beneath a gentleman.
Sturdy, useful service, like that of a loyal yeoman. His fair handwriting did Hamlet 'yeoman's service' in forging the new order.
A solemn appeal or earnest entreaty. Hamlet's forged letter framed an 'earnest conjuration' from the King.
A subordinate state that pays tribute to a stronger one. The letter calls England Denmark's faithful tributary.
A wreath of wheat symbolizing peace and plenty. The letter wishes peace to keep wearing her wheaten garland.
Time to confess one's sins and be absolved before death. The forged order denied the bearers even shriving-time.
Directing events; providential. Even in the matter of the seal, Hamlet says, 'heaven was ordinant.'
A small seal, often a ring, used to stamp wax and authenticate documents. Hamlet had his father's signet to seal the forged order.
A secretly substituted thing (originally a child swapped by fairies). Hamlet's forged order was the changeling, never detected.
Crafty intrusion; ingratiating oneself into a matter. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's deaths grew from their own insinuation.
Great and powerful adversaries. It is dangerous for lesser men to come between the deadly thrusts of mighty opposites.
Cheating, fraud, trickery. The King won the throne and threatened Hamlet's life with such cozenage.
A spreading sore or ulcer; a corrupting evil. Hamlet asks if it is not damnable to let this canker (the King) spread further evil.
An affected, foppish courtier who brings Hamlet the King's challenge and umpires the fatal duel. Hamlet mocks his empty mannered speech.
A flitting, showy insect; Hamlet's contemptuous name for the trivial, fluttering Osric.
A chattering crow (jackdaw), here meaning an empty babbler. Hamlet scorns Osric as a 'chough,' rich in land but a mere chatterer.
A soft cap or hat. Hamlet teasingly tells Osric to put his bonnet to its proper use, on his head.
One's temperament or bodily constitution. Hamlet jokes the weather is too sultry 'for my complexion,' mocking Osric's flattery.
The very model and guide of gentlemanly conduct (a 'card' is a chart). Osric so describes Laertes.
That which contains or sums up the whole. Laertes, says Osric, holds the 'continent' of every quality a gentleman could wish.
Description; a defining account. Hamlet mockingly tells Osric his 'definement' of Laertes loses nothing.
Loss; ruin. Osric's praise of Laertes 'suffers no perdition,' loses nothing, in the telling.
One's like or equal; a true counterpart. Laertes's only match, Hamlet says in parody, is his own mirror image.
A shadow; here a mere shadowy imitation. Anyone else could only trace Laertes's umbrage (shadow), nothing more.
The relevance or point of a matter. Hamlet asks Osric, 'the concernancy, sir?' — what is the point of all this praise?
The naming or mention of someone. Hamlet asks what the 'nomination' (mention) of Laertes is meant to convey.
Reputation; what is attributed to someone. Osric speaks of the imputation (high repute) laid on Laertes for his weapon.
Merit, or the reward of merit. In his 'meed' (his deserved esteem) Laertes is unequalled.
Without an equal; matchless. Laertes is said to be unfellowed with the rapier.
Prized swift horses from the Barbary Coast of North Africa. The King has wagered six Barbary horses on the duel.
Staked; wagered (Osric's affected term). Against the horses, Laertes has 'imponed' French rapiers and daggers.
Small, slender daggers. Among the stakes are six French rapiers and poniards.
The accessories or fittings that go with a weapon. The rapiers come with their assigns: girdle, hangers, and so on.
The straps or loops on a belt from which a sword hung. Osric calls the elaborate sword-straps 'carriages'; Hamlet insists they are hangers.
Osric's pretentious word for sword-hangers (properly, the mountings of a cannon). Hamlet teases that 'carriages' suits cannon, not swords.
Generous, elaborate design or fancy work. The sword-fittings are praised as of 'very liberal conceit.'
Closely related; pertinent. The word 'carriages' would be more 'german' (apt) to the matter if one carried cannon at one's side.
The time set aside for exercise. Hamlet says fencing is his usual breathing time of day, so he'll oblige.
A bird said to run about with the eggshell still on its head, a type of the half-formed upstart. Horatio mocks Osric as such a lapwing.
A worthless, frivolous era (dross is worthless scum). Hamlet condemns the drossy age that dotes on fops like Osric.
A frothy, superficial store of fashionable phrases. Hamlet says Osric's set have only a yeasty collection of trendy talk.
Carefully sifted, refined judgments. The fops' frothy chatter carries them through even the most fanned and winnowed opinions, until tested.
A misgiving; a foreboding of evil. Hamlet feels a 'gain-giving' of trouble before the duel.
Foretelling the future from omens. Hamlet says he defies augury and trusts in providence.

glossary.term: special providence in the fall of a sparrow
glossary.gloss: God's care attends even the smallest event. Hamlet voices his calm acceptance of fate before the duel.
Being prepared to meet death whenever it comes is what matters. Hamlet's resigned watchword before the fatal match.
Early; before the due time. Since no one truly owns what he leaves behind, Hamlet asks, what does it matter to die betimes?
The assembled royal company. Hamlet asks pardon of Laertes before 'this presence,' the gathered court.
Grievous mental disturbance; madness. Hamlet pleads that he wronged Laertes only through his sore distraction.
A thin metal backing set behind a gem to make it shine brighter; also a fencing sword. Hamlet puns: his own clumsiness will 'foil' Laertes, setting off his skill like a jewel.
Stand out brilliantly, blaze conspicuously. Laertes's skill will 'stick fiery off' against Hamlet's ignorance.
A large, precious pearl. The King pretends to drop an 'union' into the wine, but really drops poison.
A kettledrum, sounded with trumpets at a royal toast. The kettle is to speak to the trumpet as the King drinks.
Plain and unmistakable; able to be felt. Osric declares 'a very palpable hit.'
Drinks a toast heartily. The Queen 'carouses' to Hamlet's fortune, drinking the poisoned cup.
A handkerchief or cloth. The Queen offers Hamlet her napkin to wipe his brow.
A bird thought stupid and easily snared, a type of the dupe. Laertes, caught by his own trap, calls himself a woodcock to his own springe.
A snare or trap for catching birds. Laertes is killed 'as a woodcock to my own springe,' caught in his own treachery.
A wicked plot or treachery. Laertes confesses the foul practice has turned back on himself.
Mixed or compounded (as a potion). The poison was 'temper'd by himself' — the King brewed his own death.
A cruel arresting officer; death personified as a sheriff's sergeant strict in making his arrest. Hamlet calls death this 'fell sergeant.'
Silent actors with no lines; here, helpless onlookers. The court stand as mutes or mere audience to the bloodshed.
An ancient Roman, for whom noble suicide was honorable. Horatio, ready to drink the poison and die with Hamlet, calls himself 'more an antique Roman than a Dane.'
Happiness; here the bliss of death and release. Hamlet begs Horatio to forgo felicity awhile and live to tell his story.
A salute fired from guns. Fortinbras, back from Poland, greets the English ambassadors with this warlike volley.
Overpowers, triumphs over (as a victorious cock crows over a beaten one). The poison o'er-crows Hamlet's spirit.
A final vote or endorsement given as one dies. Hamlet gives his 'dying voice' to Fortinbras for the Danish throne.
Events; occurrences. Hamlet bids Horatio tell Fortinbras of the occurrents great and small.
Hamlet's dying words: there is nothing more to say; what follows death is unknown and unspeakable.
A heap of slain bodies (a hunting term for the day's kill). Fortinbras calls the corpse-strewn scene a 'quarry' that cries havoc.
Proclaims indiscriminate slaughter ('havoc' was the signal for no-quarter killing). The heap of dead 'cries on havoc.'

glossary.term: so jump upon this bloody question
glossary.gloss: Arriving exactly at the moment of this bloody event. Horatio notes the ambassadors and Fortinbras have come 'so jump' (so precisely on time).
Old, remembered claims to the throne. Fortinbras says he has 'some rights of memory in this kingdom' to press.
Set to the test; placed in a position of trust or office. Hamlet, had he been 'put on' (made king), would have proved most royally.
Death; one's passing. For Hamlet's 'passage,' soldiers' music and the rites of war are ordered.

chapters.1: Bitter cold on the battlements of Elsinore: for two nights running the sentries have seen a figure in armor that looks like the late King, and they bring the scholar Horatio to see it for himself. Inside, the court celebrates a swift wedding — the dead King's brother Claudius has taken both the crown and the widowed Queen — while Prince Hamlet grieves alone and Laertes and Polonius each warn Ophelia away from him. When word of the apparition reaches Hamlet, he resolves to stand the night watch himself.
chapters.2: Elsinore has become a house of watchers. Polonius sets a spy on his own son in Paris and decides Hamlet's strange transformation is thwarted love for Ophelia, while the King and Queen summon Hamlet's school friends Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to sound him out. Then a troupe of traveling players arrives at the castle, and an old speech about the fall of Troy gives Hamlet an idea.
chapters.3: Claudius and Polonius set Ophelia in Hamlet's path and listen from hiding, hoping at last to read the cause of his behavior. Hamlet, for his part, coaches the visiting players in a performance built to search the King's face, with Horatio posted to watch alongside him. As the court gathers for the play, watcher and watched close in on one another — and afterward Hamlet is summoned to his mother's private chamber.
chapters.4: Violence in the Queen's chamber gives Claudius the pretext he needs: Hamlet is to be shipped to England at once, escorted by Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. On the way to the coast Hamlet crosses the path of young Fortinbras's army, marching to fight over a patch of Poland not worth the powder. Back at Elsinore, grief begins to unmoor Ophelia, and Laertes storms home from France at the head of an angry crowd demanding answers — fury that Claudius quietly begins to bend toward a purpose of his own.
chapters.5: In a churchyard outside the castle, two gravediggers trade jokes over their spadework, and Hamlet — unexpectedly back in Denmark — falls into conversation with them over old skulls and older questions. A funeral procession interrupts the meditation and brings him face to face with the whole court. Then the foppish courtier Osric arrives with a wager from the King: a friendly fencing match, before the assembled court, between Hamlet and Laertes.

define.gloss: The space beneath the Elizabethan stage, reached by a trapdoor — when the Ghost cries 'Swear!' from under the boards, the audience heard a voice rising from the literal cellarage Hamlet jokes about.

Literally 'young hawks' — a jab at the fashionable boy-actor companies whose London vogue around 1600 was driving adult troupes like Shakespeare's own out on tour, the very reason these players have come to Elsinore.
A hanging tapestry deep enough to conceal a person, named for the Flemish weaving town of Arras — Elizabethan drama's favorite piece of eavesdropping furniture.

define.gloss: A silent mimed preview of the plot performed before the spoken play — already an old-fashioned stage convention by Shakespeare's day.
The spectators who paid a penny to stand in the open yard around the stage; Hamlet's sneer at their taste is Shakespeare teasing his own paying audience.
Swiss mercenary bodyguards, the standard protection of Renaissance royalty — Claudius calling for his Switzers shows a king who trusts hired steel over his own subjects.
An old form of 'coroner,' the officer whose inquest decided whether a death permitted Christian burial — the gravediggers are parodying the tortured logic of a real Elizabethan legal case.
The blunted fencing sword of the final match, but also the thin metal leaf set behind a jewel to make it flash — Hamlet puns on both senses when he calls himself Laertes's foil.
